sentences: This year, I have a project: a small vegetable garden behind the house.
My neighbor, Mrs. Petit, tells me: "It's easy!
You need sunshine, water, and patience.
In April, I prepare the soil.
It's a workout!
Then I plant tomatoes, lettuce, carrots, and basil.
Every day, I water my garden.
I wait.
One week, nothing.
Two weeks.
And one morning: little green leaves!
I am proud.
But snails love my lettuce.
Every morning, I find holes in the leaves.
Mrs. Petit tells me: "Put sand around the lettuce.
" It works!
In June, the tomatoes are green.
In July, they turn red.
The first red tomato, I eat it directly in the garden.
It is sweet.
Tonight, I am making a big salad with my vegetables.
My whole family eats my work.
" It's delicious!
" says my wife.
Mrs. Petit is right.
Sunshine, water, patience, and a little love.
It's one of the most famous health rules in the world: you should drink two liters of water a day, which is about eight glasses.
Apps track our glasses, graduated bottles encourage us hour by hour, and many people feel guilty for not managing to do it.
But where does this number actually come from?
Its origin is more unclear than we think.
A recommendation from the 1940s in the United States is often cited, which indeed mentioned about two and a half liters of water per day.
But the same sentence specified that a large part of this water already comes from our food.
This second half of the sentence was forgotten along the way, and only the round number survived.
This is the fate of many health advice: the nuance disappears, the slogan remains.
Because it's a fact: we eat water as much as we drink it.
A cucumber or a tomato contains more than ninety percent.
A soup, a yogurt, an orange, and even bread contribute their share.
Tea and coffee count too, contrary to a stubborn misconception: their effect on urine is far too weak to cancel out the water they contain.
Our actual needs vary greatly.
A tall person running in the summer sun does not have the same needs as a petite person sitting in an air-conditioned office.
The climate, physical activity, diet, age: everything comes into play.
Giving a single number for everyone doesn't make much sense.
The good news is that we have a remarkable measuring tool: thirst.
This mechanism, refined by millions of years of evolution, kicks in as soon as the body starts to lack water.
For the vast majority of healthy people, drinking when you're thirsty is more than enough.
A complementary indicator, not very poetic but reliable: the color of urine.
Clear, everything is fine; dark, drink more.
There are of course exceptions.
Older people feel less thirsty and need to remember to drink, especially during a heatwave.
Athletes and some sick individuals have specific needs.
But for others, there's no need to carry a giant bottle everywhere or to count your glasses anxiously.
Drink when you're thirsty, eat fruits and vegetables, and trust your body.
It's been doing this job for a very long time.

sentences: When I left to study in Lyon, my parents couldn't help me much.
Between my small scholarship and a few hours of work on Saturdays, I had about two hundred euros a month for everything else once the rent was paid: food, transportation, living.
Two hundred euros.
I smile when I think back on it, but at the time, I had to learn.
Quickly.
The first lesson was cooking.
A student who eats out, even sandwiches, burns through their budget in ten days — I found that out in the first month, along with the end-of-month panic that comes with it.
So I learned to cook, armed with a second-hand book and my grandmother's advice over the phone.

I discovered a whole new world: seasonal vegetables that cost three times less, dried legumes — lentils, chickpeas, beans — filling and almost free, the big pot on Sundays that provides four meals for the week.
My star dish, lentil curry, cost less than a euro per serving.
Ten years later, I still cook it.
The second lesson was more subtle: the small invisible expenses.
I noted down absolutely everything I spent for a month.
The result amazed me.
Coffee from the machine, snacking, little purchases that seemed insignificant: when added up, they exceeded my food budget!
It wasn't the big expenses that were ruining me, it was the tiny ones.
Since that discovery, I record my expenses for one week each quarter, just to check where the money goes.
It always slips away through the small holes.
The third lesson is the most valuable: free things.
Deprived of cinema, concerts, and restaurants, I explored what costs nothing — and the list is long.
Museums on the first Sunday of the month.
The library, this free palace.
Picnics in the park instead of on terraces.
Game nights at each other's places, with everyone bringing something.
These tight years left me with a paradox: I have never had so little money, and rarely such a rich social life.
Today, my situation is comfortable, and I don't romanticize poverty: I also remember the anxious end-of-months and postponed dental care.
But those years taught me to separate two questions that advertising tries to mix up: do I want it, or do I need it?
Desire fades.
Need, on the other hand, is surprisingly small.
We live in a society that adores youth and fears old age.
Advertising sells rejuvenation as an ideal, wrinkles are erased in images, and people talk about 'seniors' with a mix of awkward respect and discreet pity.
In this context, aging appears as a pure loss: loss of strength, beauty, usefulness, and future.
However, this view, so widespread that it seems obvious, is largely false — or at least incomplete.
For while the aging of the body is inevitable, the way we age is not.
Aging well is possible, and it resembles less a matter of luck than an art that is learned and cultivated throughout life.
Let's start with what is true in the fear.
Yes, the body changes and declines; it's a fact that no miracle powder will abolish.
But this decline can be considerably slowed down, and above all, it does not solely determine well-being.

One can take care of their aging body — by moving regularly, eating well, maintaining strength and balance — and these efforts postpone the onset of dependence much more effectively than one might think.
Healthy aging is not just a matter of genetic luck; it is prepared for, starting in maturity, through habits.
But the most striking thing in aging research is elsewhere.
When studying the most fulfilled elderly people, one discovers that they are not necessarily the most vigorous or healthiest.
The body is not the decisive factor for happiness in old age.

What distinguishes those who age happily are elements of another order: the richness of their social connections, the maintenance of curiosity and projects, the feeling of still being useful, the ability to find meaning at this stage of life rather than enduring it as a long wait.
Conversely, the great enemy of old age has a name, and it is not illness: it is loneliness.
Social isolation harms health as much as many physical ailments; it accelerates both physical and mental decline.
Societies and families that keep their elders in the fabric of relationships, who engage with them, listen to them, and integrate them, offer them the best remedy — and often the most neglected.

Aging, therefore, is an art that requires attention to two things: taking care of one's body without making it an obsession, and above all cultivating what does not age within us — curiosity, affection, the desire to learn and to pass on, the capacity for wonder.
Those who continue to learn, meet, take an interest, and create go through old age while keeping the essential alive.
One last truth emerges, a bit dizzying: the way we will age is not decided at seventy, but throughout our lives.
The friendships we maintain, the passions we nurture, the relationship we establish with the passing of time — all of this slowly prepares the elderly person we will become.
Aging well does not start in old age.
It starts now.

sentences: Before getting a job, you often have to go through a stressful step: the job interview.
I had my first interview two years ago, and I still remember my hands shaking.
To apply, I had sent my resume and a cover letter.
A few days later, the company called me to offer a meeting.
I was happy, but also very worried.
How should I introduce myself?
What should I say?
What should I wear?
A friend who had already hired people gave me some advice.
"The boss isn't looking for someone perfect," he explained to me.
He wants to know if you are motivated, honest, and if you will work well with your future colleagues.
On the day of the interview, I arrived early.
The recruiter asked me a lot of questions: about my studies, my skills, my strengths, and my weaknesses.
The hardest one was: "Why do you want this position?"
I answered honestly, in my own words.
At the end, she asked me if I had any questions.
I had prepared two; this shows that you are really interested in the job.
A week later, good news: I got hired!
Since then, I have had other interviews, and I still feel a bit nervous.
But I understood that it’s not an exam: it’s simply a conversation between two people who are trying to get to know each other.

sentences: The word 'budget' doesn't inspire enthusiasm.
It brings to mind boring spreadsheets, calculations, and the idea of deprivation.
However, creating a budget isn't a punishment: it's one of the best ways to live more peacefully with your money.
The principle is simple.
A budget is a comparison between what comes in and what goes out: on one side, the income, meaning the money you earn; on the other side, the expenses, meaning the money you spend.
As long as you don't do this calculation, you're moving forward a bit blindly.
The first step is to write down, for a month, absolutely all your expenses.
The exercise is often a surprise.
You discover that the big expenses — rent, bills — aren't the only ones that weigh heavily.
It's mainly the small daily expenses, when added up, that make the money disappear: a coffee here, a purchase there, a forgotten subscription.
Once you have these numbers in front of you, you can take action.
It's not about cutting everything out, but about making choices.
What do I really want to spend on?
What doesn't bring me any pleasure, really?
Managing your money means deciding for yourself rather than enduring the end of the month.
A good budget also includes a portion for saving, even if it's small.
Setting aside a little each month, even before spending, changes everything.
This reserve allows you to handle an unexpected event — a broken appliance, a surprise bill — without panicking or going into debt.
It would be naive to think that a budget solves all problems: when income is too low, no spreadsheet is enough.
But for most people, the real problem isn't earning more; it's knowing where the money goes.
And this clarity, curiously, doesn't make life sadder.
It brings something valuable: peace of mind.

sentences: On Tuesday, at the supermarket, my bank card didn't work.
I had a full cart and there were four people behind me.
The cashier tried twice.
"Card declined," said the machine.
I was very embarrassed.
Fortunately, I had some cash in my bag.
I was able to pay.
But I didn't understand why.
I was sure I had money in my account.
In the evening, I checked online.
My account was fine.
So what was the problem?
I called my bank.
I waited fifteen minutes with horrible music.
Then a voice said: "All our lines are busy.
Please call back later." And it hung up!
I was annoyed.
The next morning, I went straight to the agency.
I waited ten minutes, then an advisor saw me.
I explained the problem to him.
He looked at his computer for a minute.
"Ah, I see.
Your card expired at the end of last month.
We sent you a new card three weeks ago."
A new card?
I hadn't received anything.
Then I thought and understood.
There was an envelope from the bank on my desk at home.
I had never opened it.
The advisor smiled.
"It happens often, you know."
In the evening, I opened the envelope.
My new card was inside.

sentences: Six months ago, I looked at the statistics on my phone.

I was calmer.

sentences: In recent years, many French cities have been planting trees at a rate not seen in a long time.
It's not just a matter of aesthetics.
The first reason is heat.
Cities are significantly hotter than the surrounding countryside — sometimes by five to ten degrees during summer nights.
Concrete and asphalt absorb heat all day and release it at night.
This phenomenon is called the 'urban heat island'.
Trees act in two ways.
They provide shade, which is obvious.
But more importantly, they cool the air by evaporating water through their leaves, somewhat like a natural misting system.
A well-planted street can be three to six degrees cooler than a bare street.
During a heatwave, this difference is not just a comfort: it can be vital for elderly people.
The second reason concerns water.
When it rains heavily in a fully paved city, the water goes nowhere and the sewers overflow.
Planted soils absorb some of this water and reduce flooding.
Finally, there is a less measurable but real effect.
Several studies show that the presence of trees reduces stress and improves the well-being of residents.
Green neighborhoods are, on average, areas where people go out more.
All of this requires choices.
A tree in the city is expensive to plant and maintain, and sometimes parking spaces need to be removed to make room for it.
These debates are often heated in city council.
But a tree planted today will be beneficial for sixty years.

sentences: Last month, I did an exercise that I recommend to everyone: I went through twelve months of bank statements, line by line, looking only for recurring payments.
I found eleven active subscriptions.
I was actually using four of them.
There were two video services, one of which I hadn't opened in eight months.
A sports app I subscribed to in January, during a moment of enthusiasm, and used three times.
An online storage space that I had forgotten about.
A digital magazine.
A warranty on a device that I no longer owned.
The total came to seventy-three euros a month, which is nearly nine hundred euros a year.
What struck me was not the amount: it was not having noticed it.
The subscription model relies precisely on this.
Each amount is deliberately modest, below the threshold where we react.
The deduction is automatic, so it's invisible.
And there is no moment of decision: we don't choose to pay, we only choose to cancel — which requires active effort.
Companies know this perfectly well.
That's why it often takes three clicks to sign up and many more to cancel.
I canceled seven subscriptions.
The process took about forty minutes in total.
Forty minutes for six hundred euros a year: that's probably the best hourly rate of my life.
Since then, I've adopted a rule.
Every year, in January, I review my statements.
And I cancel anything I can't justify out loud.

sentences: There is a contemporary paradox: never before has cooking been so present in the media, and never has the time spent cooking been so low.
Cooking shows attract millions of viewers.
Recipes circulate in video by the thousands.
However, the time spent daily on meal preparation has significantly decreased over the past fifty years, and the share of prepared dishes in purchases has greatly increased.
Watching someone cook is not the same as cooking.
This evolution can be easily explained: longer days, commutes, and an abundant and cheap supply of ready-made meals.
It would be unfair to see this as laziness.
But it has concrete consequences.
The first is financial.
Cooking with raw ingredients remains significantly cheaper, assuming comparable quality.
The second is nutritional.
Industrial dishes contain, on average, more salt, sugar, and additives, not out of malice, but because they need to be preserved and appeal immediately.
The third is a form of autonomy.
Knowing how to cook means being able to eat well on a budget, improvise with what you have, and not be entirely dependent on what the industry offers.
However, this is not a rare talent.
Five or six techniques are enough to cover the essentials: boiling eggs, sautéing onions, cooking starches, roasting vegetables, making a vinaigrette, and preparing a soup.
With this, you can manage months of meals.
This is not gastronomy, and that is not the goal.
It is simply about knowing how to feed oneself.

sentences: I'm too old to learn that." This phrase is one of the most common, and one of the least accurate.
The adult brain retains a capacity for learning throughout life.
This phenomenon has a name, brain plasticity, and it is well established: connections reorganize based on what one practices, at thirty as well as at seventy.
That doesn't mean there are no differences.
Some things are indeed easier when young, especially acquiring a perfect accent in a foreign language.

But adults have real and underestimated advantages: they understand structures, make connections with what they already know, choose their methods, and know why they are learning — a chosen motivation is better than an imposed one.
What mainly changes are the conditions.
An adult has less time, more fatigue, and much more fear of looking foolish.
This fear is probably the main obstacle, well before age.
Research on learning provides some solid principles that are valid at any age.
Spaced repetition beats massed repetition: three times twenty minutes in a week is better than one hour on Sunday.
Testing oneself is more effective than rereading.
Trying to remember, even without succeeding, anchors more than just reviewing the text.
Finally, moderate difficulty is useful: what is too easy teaches nothing.
So the question is not whether one can still learn.
It is whether one accepts being bad for a few weeks.

sentences: For about ten years, women's sports have been experiencing rapid growth.
Competitions are attracting record audiences, stadiums are filling up, and professional clubs have been established in disciplines where they hardly existed before.
This movement can partly be explained by a simple decision: broadcasting.
For a long time, the argument against broadcasting women's competitions was the lack of an audience.
The reasoning was circular: without broadcasting, there are no spectators; without spectators, there is no broadcasting.
When major networks began broadcasting women's matches during prime time, audiences exceeded expectations, sometimes by a wide margin.
However, progress remains uneven.
Wage gaps remain significant in most disciplines.
Training resources, infrastructure, and medical support are often still inferior.
Several athletes have reported basic facilities compared to those of the men's teams in the same club.
Another topic has recently emerged: medical research.
For decades, sports physiology has been studied almost exclusively on men, and training protocols have been designed based on this.
More recent studies are finally focusing on female specifics, particularly knee ligament injuries, which are significantly more common among female athletes.
There is also the role of example, which is difficult to quantify but real.
Club registrations regularly increase after major women's competitions.
It's easier to practice a sport when you've seen someone who looks like you doing it.

sentences: Social housing plays an important role in France: it accounts for about one in six homes and houses several million people.
It is often subject to representations that are far from reality.
The first concerns the residents.
Contrary to a common belief, social housing is not only for unemployed people.
The income limits are set in such a way that a significant portion of the population is eligible, and a majority of tenants are employed.
You can find nurses, employees, teachers — that is to say, jobs that are essential for the functioning of cities where housing has become difficult.
The second concerns allocation.
It does not depend on an individual decision but on commissions that review applications based on criteria: household composition, income, length of the application, priority situations.
Waiting times are long, especially in high-demand areas, where they can be counted in years.
The reason is arithmetic: the number of applications far exceeds the number of homes that become available each year.
Construction, on the other hand, faces several obstacles: the cost of land, the length of procedures, and sometimes local opposition to projects that have been approved in principle.
This last point is revealing.
Social housing enjoys broad support in theory but encounters specific resistance in practice, neighborhood by neighborhood.
The question raised is therefore not only technical or budgetary.
It is about whether the people who make a city function should be able to live there.
The answer seems obvious until the moment comes to decide where to build.

sentences: What is the purpose of history?
We cannot change the past." This objection seems solid.
However, it is based on a false idea of what history is.
Studying history is not about memorizing dates.
It's about learning a way of reasoning, and this way applies well beyond the past.
The historian works with sources: documents, testimonies, objects.
Each source has an author, an intention, and limitations.
The same event is told differently depending on who writes it.
The job consists precisely of confronting these narratives, spotting silences, and distinguishing a fact from an opinion.
And this is exactly what we must do every day when faced with information.
Who is speaking?
In whose interest?
What is not being said?
The historical method is, in reality, an education in critical thinking.
History also teaches complexity.
Events have multiple causes; the actors are neither entirely good nor entirely bad; a decision that seems obvious today was not at the time, given the information available then.
This caution is valuable in an era that loves simple explanations.
It also makes us more humble.
By seeing how many societies believed they held a definitive truth, we put our own certainties into perspective.
There is a commonly cited phrase: "Those who ignore history are condemned to repeat it."
It is partly true, but a bit naive: history never repeats itself exactly.
Its usefulness is more subtle.
It does not predict the future.
It teaches us not to believe the first narrative we hear.

sentences: Hosting friends for dinner intimidates many people.
They hesitate, worrying about the menu, the house, and the dishes.
This anxiety often stems from a misunderstanding: it focuses on things that matter little to the guests.
When people are asked about meals they remember fondly, they rarely mention the complexity of the dishes.
They talk about the atmosphere, the conversations, and the feeling of being warmly welcomed.
That doesn't mean that food is unimportant.
But a simple and well-made dish is better than an ambitious and failed one, which also leaves the host tense and absent, stuck in the kitchen.
People whom we enjoy visiting share a few traits.
They prepare the essentials in advance, so they can be present when the guests arrive.
A stressed host makes their guests uncomfortable; a relaxed host puts them at ease.
They embrace simplicity.
Saying 'I made something easy' is more generous than a feast that turns the meal into a performance.
They think about the people, not just the meal: arranging people so that conversation flows, avoiding leaving someone isolated.
In France, there are a few useful codes to know: not arriving exactly on time, bringing something, and not getting up from the table too quickly.
But these rules serve the same purpose: common comfort.
The best advice might be the most liberating.
Guests are not coming to judge.
They come to spend time with you.

sentences: Some cities, in France and elsewhere, have made a bold choice: to make public transport completely free for users.
This experiment fuels an interesting debate.
The arguments in favor of free transport are appealing.
It removes an obstacle for low-income individuals.
It encourages people to leave their cars behind.
It eliminates the costs associated with ticket sales and enforcement.
And it sends a message: public transport is an essential service, like schools or street lighting.
However, the observed results are nuanced.
Free transport does indeed increase ridership, sometimes significantly.
But part of this increase does not come from drivers: it comes from people who previously walked or cycled and are now taking the bus.
The effect on car traffic is therefore weaker than expected.
Above all, free transport raises the question of funding.
The money from tickets must be replaced by something else: local taxes, business taxes.
However, this revenue often used to improve the network.
The risk is to end up with free transport that is insufficient.
Because what really drives people to give up their cars is not primarily the price: it's the quality.
A frequent, punctual network that goes where you want is more convincing than a free but infrequent network.
This observation does not condemn free transport, which still has a strong social meaning.
It simply reminds us of an often-forgotten truth.
A transport option that no one wants to use remains unused, even if it's free.
The real luxury in transport is not free service.
It's being able to rely on it.

sentences: For a few decades, our societies have tended to separate the ages.
Children at school, working adults at work, elderly people in dedicated residences.
Everyone increasingly lives among similar people.
In contrast to this trend, intergenerational housing projects are developing: places designed for different generations to live in the same location, not by chance, but intentionally.
The forms vary.
There is cohabitation, where a student lives with an elderly person.
There are also buildings or neighborhoods designed to mix ages, with adapted housing, shared spaces, and sometimes a daycare and a senior residence on the same site.
The idea is based on a simple observation: the needs of some meet the resources of others.
Elderly people have time, experience, and often suffer from isolation.
Young families lack time, support, and sometimes guidance.
Children benefit from the presence of available adults.
By bringing these groups together, natural exchanges are created: a helping hand, a story told, a conversation.
The initial results are encouraging, but the organizers emphasize an essential condition, the same as for any cohabitation: the framework.
Without well-thought-out shared spaces, without organized opportunities for meeting at the beginning, and without clear rules, generations can live side by side without ever crossing paths.
Geographical proximity alone does not create a bond.
These projects remain minority initiatives, limited by land availability and the difficulty of setting them up.
But they remind us of an overlooked truth.
Separating the ages is recent in human history.
For a very long time, generations simply lived together.

sentences: A new demand is sweeping through the world of work: we no longer ask our jobs just to sustain us, but to help us thrive.
Work should have meaning, align with our values, and allow us to 'realize ourselves.'
This aspiration, widely shared by younger generations, marks a break from the time when people worked primarily to live, without expecting their jobs to give meaning to their existence.
This evolution is somewhat admirable.
The refusal to spend eight hours a day on a task deemed absurd or harmful reflects a moral demand.
That employees leave a well-paid position for a more modest job they find useful is not naivety: it’s a sign that they place meaning above comfort.
However, this quest has its own dangers.
By expecting work to fulfill all our needs—material, social, and spiritual—we may be placing a burden on it that it cannot bear.
A job that disappoints then becomes not just a minor inconvenience, but a personal failure.
The disappointment is all the more intense because the expectations were high.
We must also recognize a privilege in this demand.
Seeking meaning in one’s work assumes that one has a choice.
A large part of humanity works primarily to survive, and questioning whether one’s job 'has meaning' would be a luxury for them.
The discourse on professional fulfillment sometimes overlooks this reality.
Should we then give up on this aspiration?
Certainly not.
But it might be fairer to seek meaning in several areas of life, not just in work alone.
A bearable job that leaves time and energy for what we love may be better than an all-consuming passion that leaves nothing.
Work can have meaning; it shouldn’t have to bear all the weight of it.
Expecting a job to save us is almost certainly condemning it to disappoint us.

sentences: There is a paradox unique to big cities: it is often there, surrounded by millions of human beings, that one feels the most alone.
Every day, we pass by hundreds of faces without knowing any of them.
We live just a few meters away from neighbors whose names we don't know.

This solitude in the midst of the crowd is one of the characteristic experiences of urban life, and it fuels a recurring criticism: big cities make people cold, indifferent, and strangers to one another.
This criticism is not without foundation.
In a village, everyone knows everyone, and this familiarity creates a natural mutual aid, a safety net of solidarity.
In the big city, this safety net becomes stretched.
One can go through a hardship without anyone noticing, fall ill without anyone caring.
Urban anonymity does have a shadowy side, and it would be dishonest to deny it.
But it would be just as unfair to focus only on the dark side, because this anonymity is also a form of freedom.
In the village where everyone knows each other, everyone observes each other, and the gaze of others can sometimes weigh heavily.
Those who don't fit the mold, who live differently, who want to escape a past or a reputation, find in the anonymity of the city a space to breathe.
One can be oneself there without having to explain, change one's life without the whole village commenting on it.
That is why big cities have so often attracted those whom their original environment stifled.
The artist, the outsider, the one who loves differently, the one who wants to start over: all have seen in the city not a human desert, but a promise of emancipation.
The indifference of others, so harsh when one suffers, becomes beneficial when one simply wants to live without being judged.
The anonymity of cities is therefore neither an absolute evil nor an absolute good; it is both depending on the moment in life one is in.

The challenge is not to eliminate it — one cannot know millions of people — but to create, within the vast anonymous city, small circles of familiarity: a building where people greet each other, a neighborhood where one has their bearings.
The freedom of the unknown, tempered by the warmth of a few chosen connections.

sentences: Sometimes, it only takes a detail to reveal a profound change.
Researchers have observed that the mere presence of a phone placed on a table, even when it is turned off and face down, is enough to alter the quality of a conversation.
Exchanges become more superficial, and the participants confide less, as if the object, by its mere presence, reminds us that an elsewhere is always available.
This observation, seemingly trivial, says a lot about what constant connectivity does to our relationships.
The mechanism is subtle.
Our deepest conversations require full attention and a certain vulnerability: one must feel listened to in order to dare to open up.
However, the presence of a screen, always ready to grab our attention, introduces a latent distraction.
Even when we are not looking at it, we know it is there, and this diffuse awareness is enough to hold back, shorten, and prevent the exchange from going deep.
In addition, there is a broader transformation of our relational habits.
We multiply brief contacts — a message, a reaction, a notification — at the expense of long and attentive exchanges.
We are constantly connected to dozens of people, but rarely fully present to the one in front of us.
The quantity of our interactions has exploded; their depth, however, has diminished.
We should not give in to the easy nostalgia for a golden age of conversation that may never have existed.
Screens also connect us to those who are far away and provide immense services.
The problem is not the technology itself, but the way it becomes a permanent third party, present even in our most intimate moments.
The solution does not lie in a dramatic rejection, but in a few simple and deliberate gestures: putting away your phone during a meal, a moment of sharing, or a significant time.
Creating, during the day, protected spaces where we are truly present, fully there for the other person.
For what we risk losing, due to partial presence, is not trivial: it is that quality of attention that truly connects us in a conversation.
Being fully present with someone has paradoxically become one of the rarest gifts we can offer.

sentences: We spontaneously associate reducing consumption with impoverishment, as if living with fewer possessions necessarily means living worse.
This equation seems obvious; however, it is based on a particular belief, unique to our time, that happiness depends on the quantity of things we own and consume.
Yet this belief, upon examination, proves to be more fragile than it appears.
It is not a matter of denying that meeting material needs is essential.
Lacking the essentials — food, shelter, healthcare — is true poverty, and it would be indecent to downplay it.
No sensible person claims that deprivation brings happiness.
The question is not there; it concerns what happens once the essentials are secured.
And on this point, observations converge: beyond a certain threshold, accumulating possessions hardly increases well-being.
This observation can be explained by a well-known mechanism.
We quickly get used to what we acquire.
The long-desired object, once obtained, quickly ceases to bring us joy, and a new desire takes its place.
This endless race — desiring, obtaining, getting used to it, desiring again — keeps us in a state of permanent dissatisfaction, where each acquisition only briefly alleviates a renewed lack.
Consuming more does not fill this lack; it maintains it.
From this perspective, consuming less might not be impoverishment, but rather liberation.
Breaking free from the logic of accumulation means escaping an exhausting race, regaining time, money, and attention for what truly matters.
For what makes lives rich — relationships, commitment, creativity, nature, free time — is hardly bought, and the obsession with possessing often distracts us from it.
We must be careful here of an opposite trap: turning sobriety into a new guilt-inducing morality or romanticizing lack.
Living with less only makes sense if the essentials are secured, and it would be cruel to preach frugality to those who already suffer deprivation.
Happy sobriety is a choice; imposed, it is nothing but misery.
But for those who have enough, the question deserves to be asked without prejudice: what if living better is not about having more, but about desiring differently?
Consuming less is only impoverishment if one has first confused wealth with an abundance of things.

sentences: Money doesn't bring happiness," says the proverb, to which a cynic readily adds, "but it contributes to it.
Behind this worn exchange lies a real question, to which modern research provides a more nuanced answer than a simple yes or no.
For money does indeed have a real relationship with happiness, but this relationship is neither what the proverb suggests nor what the cynic implies.
Let's start with what is firmly established: up to a certain point, money does indeed contribute to well-being.
For those who lack the essentials, an additional income changes everything.

Escaping poverty, being able to feed oneself, have a roof over one's head, receive medical care, and stop living in fear of tomorrow: at this level, money buys not happiness itself, but the end of a very concrete misery.
To claim otherwise, from the comfort of an easy life, is indecent.
But the link transforms as one rises.
Beyond the threshold where essential needs are met, each additional gain brings less and less well-being.
Doubling an already comfortable income does not double satisfaction; the effect diminishes until it becomes almost imperceptible.
Money, after a certain point, obeys a law of diminishing returns: it still matters, but less and less.
Why this exhaustion?
Partly due to the habituation already mentioned: we quickly get used to what we acquire, and the new comfort rapidly becomes the norm, ceasing to bring us joy.
Partly also because, once the essentials are secured, what makes happiness—relationships, meaning, health, time—cannot be bought.
You can buy a beautiful house, but not the affection of those who live in it.
There is something even more troubling: the way we earn and spend money matters more than the amount itself.
A demanding job that pays well can harm the happiness it claims to serve.
And research shows that we derive more satisfaction from spending on experiences or for others than from accumulating possessions.
It's not just how much we have, but what we do with it that matters.
The honest answer to the old question is therefore nuanced.
Money does not bring happiness, but its absence brings misery; it contributes, but less and less; it matters, but less than how we use it.
To despise it would be naive; to expect happiness from it would be just as naive.

sentences: Tom, this Englishman who has gone through several of these readings, has been living in Paris for years now.
Arriving with his suitcase of clichés — arrogant, undisciplined, food-obsessed French people — he gradually saw these images crack, become more nuanced, and sometimes even turn against his own.
His experience, like that of many people living between two cultures, offers a conclusion to this journey: what does prolonged exposure to another country really teach us?
Tom's first lesson was to discover that his certainties about France said as much about England as they did about France.
By finding the French 'too' attached to the state, he measured, without ever having articulated it, how much he himself took individual autonomy for granted.
By being surprised that people take two hours for lunch, he revealed his own British relationship with time and work.
Every judgment he made about France was, implicitly, a confession about what he had believed to be universal and which was merely English.
The foreigner, once again, turned out to be a mirror.
The second lesson was more subtle.

As he understood France from the inside, Tom stopped explaining differences with value judgments — 'they do it poorly' or 'they do it better' — and began to see them as coherent responses to common questions.

The French attachment to the state was no longer, in his eyes, a weakness, but a choice that had its reasons and its costs; British individualism was no longer a given, but an option among others, with its strengths and weaknesses.
Understanding the other had cured him of believing that his own way was self-evident.
The third lesson, the deepest, was a certain discomfort, but a fruitful one.
Tom was no longer quite English, nor ever quite French; he stood in a middle ground, able to see each country through the eyes of the other, but belonging fully to neither.
This position has its melancholies: one is no longer quite at home anywhere.
But it has its riches: one gains a freedom, that of no longer being a prisoner of a single way of seeing, of being able to choose, understand, and relativize.
Living between two cultures means losing a simple belonging, but gaining a perspective.
What Tom ultimately came to understand goes beyond France and England.
Encountering another culture, when experienced deeply and not as a tourist, teaches us not only about the other: it teaches us about ourselves, revealing what we took for granted.
It frees us from the illusion that our world is the only possible one, and enables us to look at it from the outside, with a mix of attachment and critical distance.
This may be the highest meaning of this journey between two neighboring cultures.
Not to decide who, between France and Great Britain, would be right — a question without answer and without interest — but to discover, through the other, the relativity and value of what is ours.
Like Tom, anyone who takes the time to understand another people returns, in essence, better equipped to understand themselves.
And that is already, for a reader learning a foreign language, the most beautiful reason to continue.

sentences: We live under observation like no generation before us.
Cameras line the streets, shops, and public transport; our phones record our movements; our activities leave traces everywhere that, when gathered, create a detailed portrait of our lives.
This surveillance, pervasive and constant, has become so commonplace that we no longer notice it.
However, it's worth pausing to consider what it changes, because living under observation is not trivial, and it subtly transforms our way of being.
First, we need to measure the scale of the phenomenon.
What distinguishes our time is not the existence of surveillance — those in power have always sought to observe people — but its extent and permanence.
It has never been possible to track the actions and movements of so many people, so continuously, so in detail, and at such a low cost.
Surveillance, once limited by its means, has become almost total, extending to areas of existence that previously escaped all scrutiny.
Being observed changes behavior, even when we have nothing to hide.
Studies confirm this: knowing we are being watched makes us more conforming, more cautious, and less spontaneous.
We monitor ourselves, anticipating the gaze of others, avoiding what might be viewed negatively.
This is not necessarily conscious; it is a subtle but profound effect.
A society where everyone knows they could be observed is a society where everyone self-censors a bit, where the freedom to be oneself, to diverge, to experiment, is quietly curtailed.
That is why widespread surveillance poses a problem that goes beyond mere privacy.
It touches on freedom itself.
A part of our freedom relies on the existence of spaces removed from observation, where one can be without being seen, think without being judged, and try without fear.
By abolishing these spaces, constant surveillance not only deprives us of intimacy; it shrinks the scope of what we dare to be and do.
An entirely observed world would be one where boldness, dissent, and simple individuality become more difficult.
One might argue that this surveillance has its reasons, often good ones: security, prevention, and the proper functioning of services.
That is true, and it is not about rejecting it outright.
But it is important not to accept it blindly, as an obvious choice without cost.
Each surveillance measure should be weighed: what real benefit does it provide, for what infringement on freedom?
Too often, surveillance is adopted for uncertain security gains, without ever measuring what we give up in return.
The question is not 'Do you have something to hide?', but 'What kind of society do we want?'
Living under observation is therefore not a fate we should endure without thinking.
It is a societal choice that engages our freedom as much as our security, and it deserves to be discussed rather than accepted by default.

Preserving spaces without observation, moments without traces, a part of life removed from scrutiny, is not about defending guilty secrets; it is about defending the very conditions for a free existence.

sentences: A disturbing fact emerges from studies on the circulation of information: falsehoods often spread faster, farther, and more widely than the truth.
A false news story can travel around the world before accurate information has even begun to spread.
This observation, which contradicts the reassuring idea that the truth will always prevail, deserves our understanding because it sheds light on much of our relationship with information.
The first reason lies in the very nature of falsehood.
Unlike the truth, which is constrained by reality, falsehood is free: it can be shaped to be exactly what spreads best.
A false news story can be more surprising, more outrageous, and more in line with what people want to believe, because nothing compels it to respect the facts.
The truth, on the other hand, is what it is, often complex, nuanced, and disappointing.
In the competition for attention, falsehood has a structural advantage: it can be optimized to please and shock, while the truth cannot.
The second reason relates to our emotions.
What spreads best is not what is true, but what evokes a strong emotion: surprise, anger, fear, indignation.
False news stories are often specifically designed to provoke these emotions, which drive people to share without thinking.
We share what moves us, even before verifying its truthfulness; and falsehood, calibrated to evoke emotion, exploits this reflex.
Emotion bypasses judgment, and it is on this bypass that false information thrives.
The third reason relates to our biases.
We are naturally inclined to believe what reinforces our convictions and to reject what contradicts them.
A false news story that aligns with what we already think will be received uncritically, shared enthusiastically, while an uncomfortable truth will be met with skepticism.
Falsehoods that flatter our prejudices thus spread within groups that share those prejudices, each person sharing it all the more willingly as it reinforces what they already believed.
Understanding these mechanisms is not enough to protect ourselves from them, but it is an essential first step.
For they suggest a rule of caution: to be wary of precisely what makes us react the most.
Information that outrages us, that delights us in seeing our opponents caught out, that confirms too well what we thought, deserves a greater degree of suspicion, not trust.
It is when we are most eager to believe and share that we should, on the contrary, stop and verify.
Falsehood spreads quickly because it exploits what is most immediate in us: our emotions, our prejudices, our laziness.
Resisting its spread therefore requires resisting ourselves, slowing down where everything pushes us to react quickly.
In a world where lies have gained the upper hand, the truth needs our vigilance to defend itself — and this vigilance begins with distrust of our own impulses.

sentences: What makes a group of individuals living side by side become a true community, rather than just a simple juxtaposition of strangers?
This question is worth asking, as our modern societies sometimes seem to have lost this community bond, producing multitudes of individuals who coexist without knowing or caring about one another.
Understanding what connects people means understanding what is precisely tending to unravel today.
A community first forms around something shared.
A place we inhabit together, a common history, shared experiences, values, an activity, a goal: these shared elements create a sense of belonging, the awareness of being part of the same 'us.'
Where there is nothing in common, there are only separate individuals; where something is shared and recognized as such, a bond is woven.
The community requires a common denominator, whether real or felt, that makes the fate of the other matter to me.
But sharing is not enough; interdependence is also necessary.
A community strengthens when its members need each other, when they help one another, when everyone relies on others and knows that others rely on them.
It is in the exchange of services, mutual support, and reciprocity that the strongest bonds are woven.
Where everyone is self-sufficient, or believes they are, the community bond atrophies: we no longer need others, so we no longer associate with them, and thus the community falls apart.
Individual autonomy, so precious, can thus, when pushed to the extreme, dissolve what connects us.
There is a third ingredient, more discreet: regular encounters, repeated presence.

Communities thrive on places and moments where people cross paths, talk to each other, and recognize one another: the village square, the café, the festival, the market, the place of worship, the association.
These meeting spaces, often modest, are the living fabric of the community; it is here that bonds are formed, news is shared, and the 'us' is recognized.
Where these places disappear, where everyone goes home without crossing paths anymore, the community loses its support and withers away.
However, these three ingredients — sharing, interdependence, and encounter — are today weakened.
Mobility disrupts attachments to a place; material autonomy reduces interdependence; private life and screens make encounters rare.

We increasingly live as independent, self-sufficient, mobile individuals, which has its advantages — more freedom, fewer constraints from the group — but it also deprives us of what the community provided: support, belonging, and the feeling of not being alone in facing life.
This observation does not lead us to naively regret the communities of the past, which were often stifling, burdensome, and intolerant of difference.
Rather, it invites us to seek ways to recreate connections in a world of individuals: through chosen commitments, associations, common projects, and meeting places to preserve or reinvent.
For while the old community had its burdens, the individual without a community has their distress.
What connects us is no longer a given; we must now want it and build it — but we need it now more than ever.

sentences: There is a rare and precious state of mind that could be called the ability to think against oneself.

It involves not just defending one's beliefs, but deliberately subjecting them to the harshest scrutiny, seeking out the strongest objections that could be raised against them, and sincerely asking oneself whether one might be wrong.
This disposition goes against all our inclinations, and perhaps that's why it represents the pinnacle of intellectual honesty, and is one of the most challenging things there is.
Our inclinations indeed lead us in the opposite direction.

We spontaneously seek what confirms our beliefs, not what contradicts them; we readily accept arguments that support us, and view with suspicion those that disturb us; we associate with those who think like us and shy away from contradiction.

This deeply ingrained tendency causes our convictions, instead of being tested, to reinforce themselves, transforming into certainties that are all the more solid because they have never been challenged.
Thinking against oneself means resisting this tendency, making the unnatural effort to seek out what could disprove us.
Why impose such an effort on oneself?
Because it is the only path to a conviction that truly matters.

An opinion that has never been confronted with its objections is not a thought, but a prejudice, even if it happens to be true; it is held out of habit, belonging, or laziness, not because it has been tested.

The one who has sought the best reasons to think differently, and maintains their position despite them, holds it in a completely different way: not as an accepted dogma, but as a conclusion that has been earned.
Thinking against oneself does not weaken solid convictions; it strengthens them by discarding those that are not.
This discipline has an additional virtue: it is the best remedy for the blindness of factions.

The one who commits to seeking what their opponent might have that is valid, to formulating the opposing position in its strongest form rather than in caricature, can no longer treat those who think differently as fools or evildoers.
They discover that disagreement often rests on reasons, not merely on the stupidity or malice of the other.
Thinking against oneself is thus a school of justice towards others, as much as it is of rigor towards oneself.
However, it is not about sinking into a universal doubt that would prohibit any conviction.
Thinking against oneself is not about thinking nothing at all, nor about changing one's mind at every objection; it is about testing one's convictions, not dissolving them.
The goal is not perpetual uncertainty, but a certainty that has paid the price of examination.
After seeking out contrary reasons and weighing their strength, one can, and must, conclude — but one concludes then with full knowledge, knowing what has been set aside and why.
It is a firmness that has gone through doubt, not one that has fled from it.
Such a discipline is demanding, and no one practices it perfectly, as it requires constantly overcoming our self-esteem, our desire to be right, our attachment to who we are.
But it is the heart of any honest intellectual life, and its very rarity makes it valuable.

In an era that rewards overt certainty and unwavering allegiance, where everyone surrounds themselves with what comforts them, making the effort to think against oneself is almost an act of resistance.

It is also the mark of a truly free spirit: not the one who never doubts, nor the one who doubts everything, but the one who has the courage to ask themselves, regarding their dearest convictions, whether it might be possible that they are wrong.

sentences: We readily imagine that words are just simple labels, neutral instruments that designate things without coloring them.
This reassuring notion is false, and its falsehood has considerable political consequences.
For naming is never an innocent act: the word we choose to designate a reality already proposes an interpretation, shapes the way we perceive it, and biases judgment even before the argument begins.
In any debate, the one who imposes their vocabulary has already, in part, won.
Let's consider the same reality described by different words.

Depending on whether we talk about 'charges' or 'contributions', 'asylum seekers' or 'illegals', 'termination of pregnancy' or 'removal of an unborn child', it’s not just the tone that changes: it’s the reality itself that appears in a different light, prompting a different reaction.
Each word carries connotations, activates associations, and suggests an evaluation.
The choice of term is not merely a dressing of thought; it is the first act that sets the stage on which everything else will play out.
This power of vocabulary explains the intensity of struggles that seem, on the surface, to be about simple words.
When one side imposes its terminology, it simultaneously imposes its way of seeing, and forces the opponent to debate in a language that is unfavorable to them.
Accepting the other’s words is already entering into their framework, reasoning according to their assumptions, and fighting on a ground they have chosen.
That’s why the most important debates often begin with a battle over the words themselves: how to name the thing we are going to discuss.
This preliminary battle, seemingly secondary, is often decisive.
There is something even more subtle.
Certain words have the power to make some realities thinkable or unthinkable.
As long as a phenomenon has no name, it remains difficult to grasp, denounce, or combat; giving it a word is to make it exist in the debate, to give it substance, and to allow it to be taken up.
Many struggles have begun with the forging of a word that finally named what everyone felt but could not express.
Conversely, the absence of a word, or the euphemism that obscures, can keep in the shadows what we prefer not to see.
Language does not merely describe the world; it decides, to some extent, what will be visible and sayable in that world.
From this power arises a common manipulation: euphemism, which softens what it names to make it acceptable.
We talk about 'collateral damage' to avoid saying deaths, 'social plan' to avoid saying layoffs, and 'strikes' to avoid saying bombings.
These words are not entirely untrue, but they anesthetize, distance us, and prevent us from feeling what the bare fact would provoke.
Euphemism is a weapon precisely because language is not neutral: it exploits the power of words to color reality, making it bearable or invisible.
Becoming aware that words are never neutral does not mean falling into a generalized suspicion where all language is manipulation.
It is to acquire vigilance: to ask ourselves, in front of the words proposed to us, what they suggest, what they hide, what framework they establish, and what interpretation they incline towards.
It is also to refuse to let others hold the monopoly on naming, to claim the right to choose one’s own words rather than submit to those imposed on us.
For to a large extent, he who controls the words controls thought — and reclaiming language is the first of freedoms.

sentences: We live in the age of infinite reproduction.
A work of art can be photographed, digitized, and distributed in millions of identical copies, accessible to everyone, everywhere, at any time.
One might think that this reproducibility would have devalued the original: why bother traveling to see a painting that can be viewed in better definition on a screen?
And yet, the opposite has happened: never have originals attracted so many crowds, and never has their value been so high.
This paradox deserves to be examined, as it reveals something profound about our relationship with authenticity.
Let's reflect on what reproduction preserves and what it loses.
A faithful reproduction retains everything that is visible in the work: the shapes, the colors, the composition.
In a sense, it provides access to the work, and this democratized access is a tremendous benefit, making art available to the greatest number of people.

But it loses something that information cannot capture: the presence of the unique object, the fact that this, precisely, is the object that the artist touched and shaped, in front of which we stand in the same space.
This presence, which the philosopher called the 'aura,' resists reproduction, because it does not depend on what the work shows, but on what it is.
What underlies this aura of the original?
First, its uniqueness and authenticity: the original is the only real object, the one that has a history, that has traversed time, that bears the mark of the hand that made it.
The reproduction, no matter how perfect, does not have this history; it is a copy without origin, detached from time and place.
In front of the original, we experience the vertigo of a real presence, the feeling of a direct contact with the creative act and with the centuries that separate us from it.
This feeling is not rational — the image is the same — but it is powerful, and it stems from the fact that we do not value only what a thing shows, but what it is.
This observation says a lot about us.
It shows that our relationship with works, and more broadly with things, is not purely informational.
We do not seek merely to see an image; we seek a connection with the real, with the authentic, with the unique.
That is why reproducibility, far from abolishing the value of the original, may have exalted it: by making images omnipresent, it has made the contact with the thing itself more precious by contrast.
The more copies abound, the more the original stands out as the only place of authentic presence.
This phenomenon goes beyond the realm of art.
In an age where everything is reproduced, simulated, and virtualized, the authentic acquires a new value, precisely because it becomes rare.
We seek the 'real' experience, the 'true' contact, the 'authentic' object, in a world saturated with reproductions and simulacra.

This quest for authenticity, so characteristic of our time, may be a reaction to widespread reproducibility: the more the world fills with copies, the more we thirst for originals, for what is unique, real, and irreplaceable.
It is not a matter of naively opposing the noble original to the contemptible copy, nor of regretting reproduction, which has democratized access to art and culture.
It is about understanding what each brings and what each loses.
Reproduction disseminates the information of the work, makes it accessible, integrates it into our lives; the original offers presence, authenticity, and contact with the real.

Both have their value, and our time, far from having to choose, enjoys both at once: it knows the works through their reproductions and rushes towards the originals to experience what no copy can provide.
This coexistence reveals that we are beings for whom real presence has a value that information, no matter how perfect, cannot replace.

sentences: There have always been poor people, and there always will be. This phrase, often spoken with an air of wisdom, expresses a fatalism that treats poverty as an inevitable aspect of the human condition, a natural fact against which it would be futile to fight.
This fatalism is convenient: it relieves one from taking action, it soothes the conscience, and it makes inaction seem like a form of clarity.
But it is based on a confusion and an error that must be exposed, because poverty is not the fatality that it is claimed to be.
First, we must distinguish between two concepts that fatalism confuses: absolute poverty and relative poverty.
Absolute poverty is the lack of essential needs — enough to eat, a place to live, access to healthcare, and to survive.
Relative poverty is having much less than others in a given society, without necessarily lacking the essentials.

These two realities are quite different, and fatalism mixes them up to seem more justified: "we will never eliminate all poverty" is plausible if it refers to relative poverty, which assumes that disparities are always possible; but it is false if it refers to absolute poverty, that of lacking essentials, which is not inevitable.
For absolute poverty, far from being a fatality, has significantly decreased in recent history, and there is nothing to prevent us from thinking that it could be eradicated.
Today, we produce enough to feed, house, and care for all of humanity; the persistence of misery is not due to a shortage of resources, but to their distribution.
That human beings lack essentials in a world that produces more than enough to meet everyone’s needs is not a natural fatality, but the result of organization, choices, and power dynamics.
Absolute misery is not inscribed in the nature of things; it is a problem that we could solve, and that we tolerate.
Fatalism regarding poverty thus serves a function: it transforms a solvable problem into an insurmountable fatality, thereby legitimizing inaction.
By presenting poverty as inevitable, it discourages any effort to combat it, it passes resignation off as wisdom, and it absolves a society that could do much more.

That is why this fatalism, under its guise of realism, is actually an ideology: it serves the interests of those who do not want to change the existing order, convincing everyone that there is nothing to be done.
"There’s nothing we can do" is the best ally of "I don’t want to do anything."
Recognizing that absolute poverty is not a fatality does not mean claiming that it would be easy to eradicate it, nor ignoring the complexity of the obstacles.

The distribution of resources faces powerful interests, real difficulties, and perverse effects that must be anticipated; combating poverty is not simple, and naive solutions can worsen the ills they claim to cure.
But difficulty is not impossibility, and recognizing that something is difficult is entirely different from declaring it fatal.
We can debate the means to reduce poverty; we cannot take refuge in the idea that it would be inevitable to avoid trying.
As for relative poverty and wealth disparities, the question is different and more complex, because some inequality may be inevitable, or even, within certain limits, acceptable.
But even there, the extent of disparities is not fatal: they have varied greatly across times and societies, which proves that they depend on choices and not on an unchanging nature.
That poverty, whether absolute or relative, persists is never a simple fatality; it is always, in part, the result of what we do and do not do.
The fatalism that naturalizes it is the first thing to combat, because as long as one considers a problem inevitable, one does not even seek to cure it.

sentences: Each of us belongs to a multitude of groups, cultures, and categories: a nation, a region, a family, a profession, a generation, sometimes multiple origins, multiple languages, multiple cultures.
Our identity is made up of these multiple affiliations, which overlap and intersect.
Yet, there is often pressure to reduce this multiplicity to a single identity, to compel everyone to choose 'who they really are,' as if one could only be one thing.
This reduction of identity to a single affiliation is one of the sources of many conflicts, and its logic must be questioned.
Let us first acknowledge the richness of multiple identities.

Being from a certain nation and a certain origin, speaking several languages, belonging to multiple cultures is not confusion or lack; it is a richness, an openness, the possibility of inhabiting multiple worlds and understanding various perspectives.

Those with multiple affiliations have a breadth of experience that those with only one do not; they can bridge different universes, translate one into another, and escape the confinement of a single vision.
The multiplicity of affiliations is not a problem to be solved, but a richness to be cultivated.
However, this richness is constantly threatened by the demand to choose.
Those with multiple affiliations are asked to say which one is the 'true' one, to choose their side, to align themselves.
This demand stems from a narrowed conception of identity, according to which one could only be one thing, belong to only one group, under penalty of betrayal or inauthenticity.
'You are this or that; you must choose': this injunction denies the reality of multiple identities, forcing one to mutilate who they are, to deny a part of themselves.
It transforms a richness into a heartbreaking dilemma.
This identity reduction is particularly dangerous because it is at the heart of many conflicts.

When everyone is compelled to define themselves by a single affiliation — a nation, a religion, an origin — the world is divided into exclusive, opposing groups, erasing everything that connects, everything that crosses borders, all shared affiliations.
Identity reduced to a single dimension becomes a principle of division and confrontation: I am this against those who are that.

Deadly identities, as one writer has termed them, arise precisely from this reduction, which makes one affiliation among others the entire identity, and pits people against each other in the name of this singular affiliation.
To this logic of reduction, we must oppose the recognition of complexity.
No one is reducible to just one of their affiliations; each person is made up of a unique intertwining of multiple affiliations that distinguishes them from all other members of each of their groups.
Two people from the same nation differ by a thousand other affiliations; what brings them together under a label does not exhaust who they are.

Recognizing this means refusing to confine others, as well as oneself, to a single identity; it means seeing in each person the irreducible complexity of their affiliations, rather than reducing them to the one that, in a given context, serves to oppose them.

Defending multiple identities against the demand to choose does not advocate for a vague identity without ties, but recognizes that attachment can be plural, that one can belong to multiple worlds without being disloyal to any.
It is to refuse that identity becomes a principle of exclusion and confrontation, and to make it what it can be: a richness made of multiple loyalties, a bridge rather than a wall.

In a world where deadly identity logics are awakening, where everyone is once again compelled to choose their side, affirming the legitimacy and richness of multiple identities is not only a truth about who we are; it is also, perhaps, a condition for peace.

sentences: Tolerance is such a universally celebrated value that people hardly take the time to clarify its meaning.
However, this meaning has become blurred, to the point that tolerance is often confused with something it is not: approval, indifference, relativism.
People believe that someone who approves of everything, who judges nothing, and who considers all beliefs to be equivalent is tolerant.
But this confusion drains tolerance of its true meaning and its difficulty.
For true tolerance does not consist of approval, but of enduring what one disapproves of — which is something entirely different and much more demanding.
Let’s reflect on the logic of tolerance.
One only tolerates what one disapproves of: there is no merit, no tolerance, in allowing what one approves of or what is indifferent to them.
Tolerance implies a disagreement, a disapproval, and consists precisely of not preventing, of enduring, of allowing to be what one disapproves of nonetheless.
He who approves does not tolerate; he adheres.
He who is indifferent does not tolerate; he does not feel concerned.
True tolerance arises from a tension: I disapprove, and yet I endure; I judge that the other is wrong, and yet I respect his right to live according to his beliefs.
Without this tension, there is no tolerance, but something else.
This clarification has important consequences.
First, it shows that tolerance does not require one to renounce their beliefs or judgments.
One can be firmly convinced that the other is wrong, disapprove of their beliefs or choices, and still tolerate them, meaning respecting their right to live according to them.
Tolerance does not require believing that everything is equal, that no one is wrong; it requires enduring what one considers to be an error, out of respect for the freedom of others.
Confusing tolerance with relativism is to mistakenly believe that to tolerate, one must renounce judgment — whereas it is precisely because one judges that one can tolerate.
This conception also reveals the true difficulty of tolerance, which its relativist version obscures.
It is easy to 'tolerate' what is indifferent to us or what we approve of; it is difficult to tolerate what offends us, what we disapprove of, what contradicts our dearest convictions.
True tolerance is measured there, by its capacity to endure what displeases, not by celebrating what pleases.

And this difficulty explains why tolerance is so rare, so often invoked, and so little practiced: for it is costly to allow what one judges to be bad, to respect the freedom of those who misuse, in our view, their freedom.
Tolerance, however, has its limits, which its relativist version cannot conceive.

If tolerating means enduring what one disapproves of out of respect for the freedom of others, then tolerance finds its limit where this freedom destroys that of others, where what one would tolerate would end tolerance itself.
One cannot tolerate, in the name of tolerance, what aims to destroy the coexistence of freedoms: there is a legitimate intolerance towards what threatens the very conditions of tolerance.

This paradox — that tolerance cannot tolerate everything, under penalty of destroying itself — only appears if one understands tolerance as respect for freedom, not as indifferent approval of everything.

True tolerance is therefore a difficult and paradoxical virtue: to endure what one disapproves of, to respect the freedom of those who misuse their freedom, while refusing to tolerate what would destroy tolerance.

It is neither the relativism that no longer dares to judge, nor the indifference that feels unconcerned, but the demanding effort to hold together the firmness of one’s convictions and the respect for the freedom of others.

In a world of incompatible beliefs, where everyone considers the other to be misguided, this kind of tolerance — which judges without oppressing, which disapproves without persecuting — is perhaps the most precious and the most fragile condition for peaceful coexistence.
It does not require ceasing to believe that one is right; it requires allowing the other the right to believe that he is right too.

sentences: Our time is one of speed.
Everything is accelerating: transportation, communication, exchanges, the pace of work and life.
We want everything faster: immediate responses, instant deliveries, results without delay.
Slowness has become a flaw, almost a fault; efficiency is measured by speed; anyone who takes their time is suspected of wasting ours.
This valorization of speed, so characteristic of modernity, seems obvious.
But it is worth questioning, because this continuous acceleration has a price that we pay without always being aware of it.
First, let’s acknowledge what is legitimate and beneficial about speed.
It has freed us from many painful slownesses, saved us precious time, and made exchanges and meetings possible that a slower existence would have prohibited.
Going fast is not inherently bad; it is often progress, saving us from unnecessary waits, tedious distances, and frustrating delays.
Praising slowness while forgetting what speed has brought us would be a nostalgic pose, blind to the burdens from which acceleration has freed us.
Speed, in many cases, is a conquest.
But acceleration becomes problematic when it becomes a value in itself, a permanent demand, a rhythm imposed on everything.
For not everything in life benefits from being accelerated; some things, on the contrary, become distorted or lost when rushed.
A deep conversation, a friendship, a work of art, a thought, a true pleasure, requires time; they cannot be hurried without falling apart.

Wanting to accelerate everything, applying the demand for speed to everything, risks losing what can only be given by slowness: depth, maturation, attention, everything that can only be done well by taking one’s time.
Generalized acceleration sacrifices what needs duration.
There is more.
This continuous acceleration deprives us of the present itself.
Always hurried, focused on what is coming, busy trying to save time, we are never quite where we are, in the moment we are living.
We rush through our existence, without stopping to savor it, running towards a future that, barely reached, gives way to another.
Speed makes us live in perpetual anticipation, never in presence; it steals the present from us in favor of a constantly elusive future.
In our eagerness to save time, we lose the time we are living, the only time we truly have.
There is a deep irony in our relationship with speed.
We accelerate to save time; but the time we gain, we do not savor, we immediately fill it with new activities, new rushes.
Speed does not give us more free time; it intensifies the filling of our time, making us do more in the same timeframe, without ever returning the leisure it promised.
We are faster and more rushed than ever, more efficient and more overwhelmed, gaining time that we immediately lose.
Acceleration does not lead to rest, but to an endless race, where we always run faster without ever arriving.
Reclaiming a healthy relationship with time does not mean giving up all speed, nor advocating for a generalized slowness that would be equally absurd.

It is about discerning what benefits from being accelerated from what requires time, creating, in a fast life, spaces for slowness, and regaining the ability to be present to what we are living rather than always being turned towards what is coming.
It is about refusing for speed to become an absolute value, resisting the injunction to always go faster, and reclaiming one’s time rather than enduring it.
For a life is not more successful for being faster; it is successful for being fully lived, and there are essential things that only slowness allows us to savor.
Living fast does not mean living more; it often means missing out on one’s life while believing one is gaining it.
