sentences: What holds a society together?
What unites a multitude of individuals, often different, sometimes opposed, into a lasting, cooperative whole rather than a dust of isolated beings?
This question, which runs through all social thought, does not have a simple answer, and the overly simplistic responses — force, interest — prove to be insufficient.
To explore what holds a society together is to discover invisible links, deeper than constraint or calculation, without which no sustainable communal life would be possible.
One might think that force is enough: a society would hold together through constraint, through the power that represses and punishes.
But we have seen that power itself rests on something other than force, on narratives, on consent, on belief in its legitimacy.

Force alone does not hold a society together; it can constrain for a time, but a society that would only hold together through constraint would be precarious, constantly threatened, incapable of the spontaneous cooperation without which communal life falls apart.
Force may explain why there is no revolt; it does not explain why we cooperate, why we trust each other, why we hold together.
One could then invoke interest: a society holds together because everyone finds their benefit in it, because cooperation is advantageous, because it is rational to live together rather than alone.
This explanation, deeper than that of force, captures a part of the truth: societies do indeed rest, in part, on mutual interest, on the advantages of cooperation.
But it is still insufficient.

For interest alone does not establish the trust without which cooperation is impossible; it does not explain why individuals respect their commitments even when it would be advantageous to betray them, why they trust each other, why they sometimes place the common good above their own interest.
A society of pure calculators, each seeking only their own advantage, would fall apart, for no one could trust anyone.
Interest presupposes, to function, a trust that it does not suffice to produce.
So what holds a society together, beyond force and interest?
Invisible links, deeper ones, that are hard to name but whose importance we measure when they are lacking.

There is trust, this fragile link that allows us to count on each other, without which neither exchange, nor cooperation, nor communal life is possible; a society where trust collapses falls apart, regardless of the force that constrains it and the interest that binds it.
There are shared values, these common representations of what is just, good, desirable, which give individuals a common world, a language, reference points.
There is the sacred, what we have mentioned, those things held to be intangible, those shared absolutes that found belonging to the same community.
There is the common narrative, the story that a society tells about itself, which connects its members in a shared 'us'.
These invisible links have in common that they arise not from constraint or calculation, but from belief, feeling, belonging.
They are not decreed, they are not imposed by force, they are not reduced to interest; they are woven slowly, transmitted, maintained, and undone when we cease to care for them.

A society holds together by these fragile links as much as by its visible institutions; and when they fray — when trust collapses, when shared values dissolve, when nothing is held sacred anymore, when the common narrative falls apart — no force or interest is enough to keep together what is no longer connected.
Societies do not only die from their visible conflicts; they also die, more silently, from the erosion of the invisible links that held them.
Understanding what holds a society together is thus to recognize the importance of these links that modernity, enamored with force and interest, tends to neglect.

It is to understand that trust, shared values, the sacred, the common narrative, are not archaic survivals that a rational society could do without, but the very conditions of communal life, without which neither force nor interest is sufficient to keep people together.
And it is to measure the fragility of these links, the necessity of caring for them, the peril of allowing them to erode.
A society is never guaranteed to last; it rests on invisible links that must be constantly maintained, and whose erosion, more than any external threat, puts it at risk.
Caring for what connects us — trust, values, a sense of the common good — is perhaps the most essential, and the most neglected, task of all social life.

alignments.french: Qu'est-ce qui fait tenir une société ?
Qu'est-ce qui unit une multitude d'individus, souvent différents, parfois opposés, en un ensemble qui perdure, coopère, forme un tout plutôt qu'une poussière d'êtres isolés ?

alignments.french: Sonder ce qui tient une société, c'est découvrir des liens invisibles, plus profonds que la contrainte ou le calcul, sans lesquels aucune vie commune durable ne serait possible.
alignments.english: To explore what holds a society together is to discover invisible links, deeper than constraint or calculation, without which no sustainable communal life would be possible.

alignments.french: On pourrait croire que la force suffit : une société tiendrait par la contrainte, par le pouvoir qui réprime et punit.
alignments.english: One might think that force is enough: a society would hold together through constraint, through the power that represses and punishes.

alignments.french: Mais nous avons vu que le pouvoir lui-même repose sur autre chose que la force, sur des récits, sur le consentement, sur la croyance en sa légitimité.
alignments.english: But we have seen that power itself rests on something other than force, on narratives, on consent, on belief in its legitimacy.

alignments.french: La force seule ne fait pas tenir une société ; elle peut contraindre un temps, mais une société qui ne tiendrait que par la contrainte serait précaire, sans cesse menacée, incapable de la coopération spontanée sans laquelle la vie commune se défait.
alignments.english: Force alone does not hold a society together; it can constrain for a time, but a society that would only hold together through constraint would be precarious, constantly threatened, incapable of the spontaneous cooperation without which communal life falls apart.

alignments.french: La force explique peut-être qu'on ne se révolte pas ; elle n'explique pas qu'on coopère, qu'on se fasse confiance, qu'on tienne ensemble.
alignments.english: Force may explain why there is no revolt; it does not explain why we cooperate, why we trust each other, why we hold together.

alignments.french: On pourrait alors invoquer l'intérêt : une société tiendrait parce que chacun y trouve son compte, parce que la coopération est avantageuse, parce qu'il est rationnel de vivre ensemble plutôt que seul.
alignments.english: One could then invoke interest: a society holds together because everyone finds their benefit in it, because cooperation is advantageous, because it is rational to live together rather than alone.

alignments.french: Cette explication, plus profonde que celle de la force, saisit une part de vérité : les sociétés reposent bien, pour une part, sur l'intérêt mutuel, sur les avantages de la coopération.
alignments.english: This explanation, deeper than that of force, captures a part of the truth: societies do indeed rest, in part, on mutual interest, on the advantages of cooperation.

alignments.french: Car l'intérêt seul ne fonde pas la confiance sans laquelle la coopération est impossible ; il n'explique pas pourquoi les individus respectent leurs engagements même quand il serait avantageux de les trahir, pourquoi ils se font confiance, pourquoi ils placent parfois le bien commun au-dessus de leur intérêt.
alignments.english: For interest alone does not establish the trust without which cooperation is impossible; it does not explain why individuals respect their commitments even when it would be advantageous to betray them, why they trust each other, why they sometimes place the common good above their own interest.

alignments.french: Une société de purs calculateurs, chacun ne cherchant que son avantage, se déferait, car nul ne pourrait se fier à personne.
alignments.english: A society of pure calculators, each seeking only their own advantage, would fall apart, for no one could trust anyone.

alignments.french: L'intérêt suppose, pour fonctionner, une confiance qu'il ne suffit pas à produire.
alignments.english: Interest presupposes, to function, a trust that it does not suffice to produce.

alignments.french: Qu'est-ce donc qui tient une société, par-delà la force et l'intérêt ?
alignments.english: So what holds a society together, beyond force and interest?

alignments.french: Des liens plus invisibles, plus profonds, que l'on peine à nommer mais dont on mesure l'importance quand ils viennent à manquer.
alignments.english: Invisible links, deeper ones, that are hard to name but whose importance we measure when they are lacking.

alignments.french: Il y a la confiance, ce lien fragile qui fait qu'on peut compter les uns sur les autres, sans lequel ni l'échange, ni la coopération, ni la vie commune ne sont possibles ; une société où la confiance s'effondre se défait, quels que soient la force qui la contraint et l'intérêt qui la lie.
alignments.english: There is trust, this fragile link that allows us to count on each other, without which neither exchange, nor cooperation, nor communal life is possible; a society where trust collapses falls apart, regardless of the force that constrains it and the interest that binds it.

alignments.french: Il y a les valeurs partagées, ces représentations communes de ce qui est juste, bien, désirable, qui donnent aux individus un monde commun, un langage, des repères.
alignments.english: There are shared values, these common representations of what is just, good, desirable, which give individuals a common world, a language, reference points.

alignments.french: Il y a le sacré, ce que nous avons évoqué, ces choses tenues pour intangibles, ces absolus partagés qui fondent l'appartenance à une même communauté.
alignments.english: There is the sacred, what we have mentioned, those things held to be intangible, those shared absolutes that found belonging to the same community.

alignments.french: Il y a le récit commun, l'histoire qu'une société se raconte sur elle-même, qui relie ses membres en un même « nous ».
alignments.english: There is the common narrative, the story that a society tells about itself, which connects its members in a shared 'us'.

alignments.french: Ces liens invisibles ont ceci de commun qu'ils relèvent non de la contrainte ni du calcul, mais de la croyance, du sentiment, de l'appartenance.
alignments.english: These invisible links have in common that they arise not from constraint or calculation, but from belief, feeling, belonging.

alignments.french: Ils ne se décrètent pas, ne s'imposent pas par la force, ne se réduisent pas à l'intérêt ; ils se tissent lentement, se transmettent, s'entretiennent, et se défont quand on cesse d'en prendre soin.
alignments.english: They are not decreed, they are not imposed by force, they are not reduced to interest; they are woven slowly, transmitted, maintained, and undone when we cease to care for them.

alignments.french: Une société tient par ces liens fragiles autant que par ses institutions visibles ; et quand ils se délitent — quand la confiance s'effondre, quand les valeurs communes se dissolvent, quand plus rien n'est tenu pour sacré, quand le récit commun se défait —, aucune force ni aucun intérêt ne suffit à maintenir ensemble ce qui n'est plus relié.
alignments.english: A society holds together by these fragile links as much as by its visible institutions; and when they fray — when trust collapses, when shared values dissolve, when nothing is held sacred anymore, when the common narrative falls apart — no force or interest is enough to keep together what is no longer connected.

alignments.french: Les sociétés ne meurent pas seulement de leurs conflits visibles ; elles meurent aussi, plus silencieusement, de l'effritement des liens invisibles qui les tenaient.
alignments.english: Societies do not only die from their visible conflicts; they also die, more silently, from the erosion of the invisible links that held them.

alignments.french: Comprendre ce qui tient une société, c'est donc reconnaître l'importance de ces liens que la modernité, éprise de force et d'intérêt, tend à négliger.
alignments.english: Understanding what holds a society together is thus to recognize the importance of these links that modernity, enamored with force and interest, tends to neglect.

alignments.french: C'est comprendre que la confiance, les valeurs partagées, le sacré, le récit commun, ne sont pas des survivances archaïques dont une société rationnelle pourrait se passer, mais les conditions mêmes de la vie commune, ce sans quoi ni la force ni l'intérêt ne suffisent à faire tenir les hommes ensemble.
alignments.english: It is to understand that trust, shared values, the sacred, the common narrative, are not archaic survivals that a rational society could do without, but the very conditions of communal life, without which neither force nor interest is sufficient to keep people together.

alignments.french: Et c'est mesurer la fragilité de ces liens, la nécessité d'en prendre soin, le péril de les laisser se déliter.
alignments.english: And it is to measure the fragility of these links, the necessity of caring for them, the peril of allowing them to erode.

alignments.french: Une société n'est jamais assurée de durer ; elle repose sur des liens invisibles qu'il faut sans cesse entretenir, et dont l'effritement, plus que toute menace extérieure, la met en péril.
alignments.english: A society is never guaranteed to last; it rests on invisible links that must be constantly maintained, and whose erosion, more than any external threat, puts it at risk.

alignments.french: Prendre soin de ce qui nous relie — la confiance, les valeurs, le sens du commun — est peut-être la tâche la plus essentielle, et la plus négligée, de toute vie en société.
alignments.english: Caring for what connects us — trust, values, a sense of the common good — is perhaps the most essential, and the most neglected, task of all social life.

sentences: I had a toothache for two weeks.
At first, it was a small pain, only when I drank something cold.
I knew I had to go to the dentist.
But I don't like the dentist.
So I waited.
I took pain medication and avoided cold drinks.
After ten days, the pain got stronger.
One night, I couldn't sleep at all.
The next morning, I called.
The secretary offered me an appointment three weeks later.
"Three weeks?"
"But it hurts a lot!"
"There is a cancellation tomorrow at eight o'clock.
Does that work for you?"
I said yes immediately.
In the waiting room, I was as nervous as a child.
The dentist looked at my tooth for two minutes, then he took an X-ray.
"You have a fairly deep cavity.
If you had come earlier, it would have been simple.
Now, it's a bit more work, but it is still repairable."
He gave me an injection, then he worked for forty minutes.
It wasn't pleasant, but I hardly felt anything.
As I was leaving, he told me a phrase that I haven't forgotten: "A tooth that hurts never heals on its own."
Since then, I go twice a year.
We often conceive of morality as a set of rules: do not lie, do not steal, do not harm, keep your promises.
To be moral, in this view, would mean knowing these rules and following them; the moral person would be one who obeys the rules, while the immoral person would be one who transgresses them.
This conception has its strengths and conveniences: it provides clear guidelines, specific prohibitions, and an apparently simple criterion for right conduct.
But it may be insufficient, and we must ask whether morality really reduces to rules, or if it requires something that rules cannot capture.
Let us first acknowledge what rules have that is useful and necessary.

They provide stable reference points, valid for everyone, independent of circumstances and individuals; they protect against arbitrariness, against the rationalizations through which one justifies their faults, and against the weakness that yields to temptations.
A morality without rules, which would decide everything on a case-by-case basis according to circumstances, would risk arbitrariness, complacency, and uncertainty.
Moral rules have the virtue of establishing firm limits, prohibitions that are non-negotiable, a foundation upon which conduct can rely.
It would be naive to want a morality without any rules.
But rules also have their limits, as moral experience reveals.

First, they cannot foresee all cases; life presents situations that no rule had anticipated, cases where rules contradict each other, where applying one means violating another, and where following the rule to the letter would produce an injustice.
Should the rule 'do not lie' be followed when lying would save a life threatened by a criminal?
Difficult cases, where rules are insufficient and judgment is necessary, reveal that morality cannot be reduced to the mechanical application of rules.
Beyond rules, there needs to be a judgment that knows how to apply them, weigh them, and sometimes exceed them.
Furthermore, and more profoundly, following rules is not enough to be moral in the fullest sense.
One can respect all rules out of calculation, fear, or conformity, without any real virtue; one can refrain from lying, stealing, or harming only out of fear of consequences, without any goodness.
In contrast, true morality seems to demand more than mere adherence to rules: an inner disposition, a goodness, an attention to others, a generosity that exceeds what any rule prescribes.
The rule states what should not be done; it does not articulate positive goodness, generosity, or love for one's neighbor, which are nonetheless at the heart of moral life.
One can follow all the rules and still remain a mediocre being; one can, by sometimes transgressing the letter of a rule, demonstrate a higher goodness.
That is why a long moral tradition has emphasized not rules, but virtues, character, and inner disposition.
What matters, from this perspective, is not so much following rules as being a certain kind of person: just, good, courageous, generous, capable of discernment.
Virtue is not obedience to rules, but an acquired disposition, a way of being that inclines toward good, a character shaped by habit and education.
The virtuous person does good not because a rule commands it, but because they are so disposed; they do good with precision, in concrete situations, through a discernment that no rule can replace.
The morality of virtues shifts the focus from rules to character, from obedience to being.
The truth may lie in the complementarity of these approaches.

Rules are necessary, as reference points, as safeguards, as a foundation; but they are not sufficient, as they cannot foresee everything, nor can they replace positive goodness, nor the judgment that applies them.

Morality requires both rules and the discernment that knows how to apply them, prohibitions and the virtue that transcends them toward positive good, obedience to rules and the inner disposition that alone makes one truly moral.
Reducing morality to rules is to mutilate it, forgetting its heart, which is a certain quality of the soul; but rejecting all rules in the name of virtue alone opens the door to arbitrariness.
Moral wisdom holds both: to follow just rules, but with the discernment and goodness that exceed them — for being moral is not just about obeying, but about becoming a certain kind of being.

Good evening!

sentences: Last year, my friend Karim asked me to lend him three hundred euros.
His car was broken down and he needed an urgent repair to get to work.
I hesitated.
Not because I didn't trust him, but because I had heard a lot of stories: friends who argue over money, families that no longer speak to each other.
Lending money is never just about money.
It's also about relationships.
In the end, I said yes.
But we did something important: we talked clearly beforehand.
We decided together: three hundred euros, to be repaid in three installments of one hundred euros each month.
Karim even wrote it in a message.
Some people find it cold between friends.
I think the opposite.
The discomfort always comes from the uncertainty: when no one knows when or how the money will be paid back.
Karim paid me back the first two months without any problem.
In the third month, he sent me a message: 'Can I pay you back the hundred euros in two weeks?
I had a bill.'
He had warned me, so it wasn't a problem.
He paid me back everything in four months instead of three.
Today, we are still friends.
And I believe we have remained friends precisely because we dared to talk about money at the beginning.

sentences: We like to believe that evil, great evil, the kind associated with atrocities and mass crimes, is the work of monsters, of exceptionally cruel beings, radically different from us.
This belief is reassuring: it places a clear boundary between evil and us, it makes criminals a separate species, it protects us from the unsettling thought that we too could be capable of such acts.
But this reassuring belief may be false, and one of the most disturbing lessons of recent history is that great evil is often committed not by monsters, but by ordinary men.
This truth, difficult to accept, deserves to be confronted, as it sheds harsh light on the fragility of civilization and our own.

The observation of great mass crimes has revealed a disconcerting reality: among those who committed or allowed them, a majority were not sadists, perverts, or monsters, but ordinary men — family fathers, conscientious employees, people who, under different circumstances, would have led mundane and honest lives.
They did not act out of exceptional cruelty, demonic hatred, but out of conformity, obedience, careerism, cowardice, and a lack of reflection.

The evil they committed was not commensurate with their mediocrity; it is this contrast between the enormity of the crimes and the banality of their authors that struck observers, and which has been termed the banality of evil.
This expression, often misunderstood, does not mean that evil is trivial, nor that crimes are excusable.

It refers to the fact that the perpetrators of great crimes can be ordinary men, that extreme evil can be committed by people who are not monsters, but who, under certain circumstances, influenced by certain mechanisms — obedience to authority, conformity, disempowerment, lack of reflection — become capable of the worst.

Evil does not necessarily require extraordinary wickedness; it can arise from ordinary dispositions and circumstances, from cowardice, conformity, refusal to think, which are within the reach of almost everyone.
This truth is unsettling precisely because it abolishes the reassuring boundary between evil and us.
If great evil were the work of monsters, we would be safe from it, separated from them by a difference in nature.

But if it is committed by ordinary men, under the influence of ordinary mechanisms, then we can no longer believe ourselves to be safe; we must consider that we too, in certain circumstances, could become capable of it.
This thought is unbearable, and that is why we resist it, preferring to believe that we would have remained, we, on the right side.

But this resistance is dangerous, because it is precisely by believing ourselves to be safe that we lower our guard, that we do not monitor within ourselves the dispositions that could lead to the worst.
Recognizing ordinary evil does not excuse criminals, as if their banality justified them; rather, it makes us more vigilant, towards others and towards ourselves.

It invites us to monitor within ourselves the dispositions that make evil possible: blind obedience to authority, conformity that follows the group, the shifting of responsibility onto others, the refusal to think for oneself, the cowardice that does not dare to resist.
It is these ordinary dispositions, more than any exceptional wickedness, that pave the way for the worst.

And to protect ourselves against evil is not to believe ourselves to be of a different species than its authors, but to cultivate within ourselves what resists these mechanisms: the courage to disobey the unjust, the independence that refuses conformity, the responsibility that does not shift, the thought that does not abdicate.
The lesson of ordinary evil is, paradoxically, a lesson in responsibility.

For if evil were the work of monsters, we would have nothing to do but distinguish ourselves from them; but if it can arise in any ordinary person, due to ordinary circumstances and dispositions, then vigilance is our responsibility.

Defending civilization against the barbarism that threatens it is not just about fighting external monsters; it is about monitoring the ordinary dispositions within ourselves and around us that make evil possible, cultivating courage, independence, responsibility, and thought, which alone can resist it.

Ordinary evil teaches us that the line between civilization and barbarism does not run between people, but within each of them — and that it is through each individual, with vigilance and courage, that this line is defended or lost.

sentences: We will die; that is a certainty.
But does something of us remain after our death, and if so, what?

This question, which extends our reflection on finitude, does not concern the survival of the soul here, about which we have seen we cannot decide, but a more modest and certain survival: what we leave in the world, in others, in what outlives us.
For even if we do not believe in life after death, it is undeniable that something of us remains, and it is worth asking what this survival is and what meaning it gives to our mortal existence.
First, we leave a mark on others, on those we have known, loved, and influenced.
Our influence on the beings we have been close to does not die with us; it remains in them, in what we have transmitted, taught, given to them, in the way we have shaped them.
Parents live on in their children, teachers in their students, each in those they have touched.
This survival is not nothing: it is real, it extends our existence beyond our death, in the imprint we have left on other lives.
We live on after our death in memory, in influence, in what we have passed on to those who survive us.
Some of us also leave behind works: creations, achievements, contributions that endure after we are gone.

The artist survives in their work, the thinker in their thoughts, the builder in what they have built; and even the humblest leave something behind — a skill passed on, a contribution to a collective effort, a part of what humanity has accomplished.
This survival in works, when it occurs, can be lasting, far outliving our existence, extending us into the centuries.
But it is not reserved for great creators; everyone, in their own way, contributes to what humanity builds and transmits, thus leaving a part of themselves in the common world.
Finally, we leave the world itself, as marked by our actions.
Each of us, through our lives, contributes to creating the world we leave to those who come after; our actions, our choices, our way of living, shape, however slightly, the world we pass on.
This kind of survival is diffuse, often anonymous, but real: the world after us bears the marks of what we have done, for better or for worse.
We are responsible for what we leave behind, for the world we transmit, for our contribution to what the existence of those who follow us will be.
What value should we assign to this survival in others, in our works, in the world?
It does not fully console us for death, because it is not our personal survival; it is not us who survive, but our mark, our influence, our work.
We will no longer be there to enjoy it, and this survival does not make us immortal.

However, it nonetheless gives meaning to our mortal existence by connecting it to what transcends and prolongs it; it places us in a continuity that exceeds our individual lives, allowing us to participate in something larger and more enduring than ourselves.
Living with the knowledge that we will leave a mark, that we contribute to what will survive, gives mortal life a significance that surpasses its duration.
This thought of what we leave behind has an ethical dimension.
For if we survive in what we leave, then what we leave matters, and we are responsible for it.

Living with the thought of what we will leave — in others, in our works, in the world — means living with the concern of leaving something good, of contributing positively, and not leaving behind ruins or harm.
The awareness of what we leave connects us to the future, makes us responsible for what we pass on, and gives our lives a direction that goes beyond our immediate self-interest.
We do not live only for ourselves, within the limited time of our existence; we also live for what we will leave behind, in the mark we will extend beyond our death.

And perhaps this is a way to give meaning to our mortal condition: not to deny death, but to live in such a way that what we leave behind is worth having been left — that our passage, however brief, adds something good to the world rather than impoverishing it.

sentences: A large French city is studying the possibility of making public transport free for all residents.
The mayor explains that this measure could reduce pollution and help families with a limited budget.
According to him, fewer cars on the streets means cleaner air and less noise.
The project is not new.
Several cities in Europe have already tested free transport, with different results.
In some cities, the number of passengers has increased a lot, which has created very crowded buses and trams during rush hour.
In other cities, the results have been more modest, but residents appreciated paying less each month.
The residents of the city are divided on this idea.
Some find the project excellent.
They think that free transport will encourage more people to leave their cars at home.
A young student explains that she already uses the bus every day to go to university, and that free transport would allow her to save a lot of money each month.
Other residents are more cautious.
They wonder who will pay for this change.
Making public transport free is expensive for the city, and money has to be found somewhere.
A downtown shopkeeper thinks that local taxes will increase to make up for the loss of revenue from bus and metro tickets.
The city council has organized several public meetings to discuss the project with the residents.
During these meetings, transport experts presented figures and studies on cities that have already adopted free transport.
They explained the benefits, such as reducing pollution, but also the challenges, like maintaining vehicles and hiring new drivers.
The mayor promised that a final decision will be made next year, after a long period of study and discussion with the citizens.
A survey will also be organized to know the general opinion of the population before the final vote in the city council.
In the meantime, the city announced a first change: transport will be free on weekends for the next three months, as a trial.
This test will measure the real impact on the number of passengers and on car traffic in the downtown area.
The results of this trial will be presented publicly at the end of the year.
Other French cities are closely following this project.
If the trial is a success, several mayors have already announced that they too would consider making transport free in their own municipalities.
For now, everyone is eagerly awaiting the first results.

So they went from jeweler to jeweler, searching for a piece similar to the other, consulting their memories, both sick with grief and anxiety.
They found, in a shop at the Palais-Royal, a diamond necklace that seemed completely similar to the one they were looking for.
It was worth forty thousand francs.
They would let it go for thirty-six thousand.
So they asked the jeweler not to sell it for three days.
And they made it a condition that it would be bought back for thirty-four thousand francs if the first one was found before the end of February.
Loisel had eighteen thousand francs that his father had left him.
He would borrow the rest.
He borrowed, asking for a thousand francs from one, five hundred from another, five louis here, three louis there.
He made promissory notes, took on ruinous commitments, dealt with usurers, and all kinds of lenders.

He jeopardized the rest of his life, risked his signature without even knowing if he could honor it, and, terrified by the anxieties of the future, by the dark misery that was about to fall upon him, by the prospect of all the physical deprivations and all the moral tortures, he went to find the new necklace, depositing thirty-six thousand francs on the jeweler's counter.

sentences: Another clue.
This fossilized body was not the only one in the immense ossuary.
Other bodies were encountered with every step we took in this dust, and my uncle could choose the most wonderful of these samples to convince the skeptics.
In truth, it was an astonishing sight to see these generations of men and animals mingled in this cemetery.
But a serious question arose that we dared not resolve.
Had these living beings slipped through a convulsion of the earth to the shores of the Lidenbrock sea, while they were already reduced to dust?
Or did they rather live here, in this underground world, under this artificial sky, being born and dying like the inhabitants of the earth?
Until now, only the sea monsters, the fish, had appeared alive to us!
Was some man from the abyss still wandering on these deserted shores?
For another half hour, our feet trod on these layers of bones.
We moved forward, driven by an intense curiosity.
What other wonders did this cave hold, what treasures for science?
My gaze was prepared for all surprises, my imagination for all astonishments.
The shores of the sea had long since disappeared behind the hills of the ossuary.
The reckless professor, caring little about getting lost, was leading me far away.
We advanced silently, bathed in electric waves.
By a phenomenon I cannot explain, and thanks to its complete diffusion at that time, the light illuminated the various faces of the objects uniformly.
Its focus no longer existed at a specific point in space and it produced no shadow effect.
One could have believed it was midday in the middle of summer, in the equatorial regions, under the vertical rays of the sun.
All vapor had disappeared.
The rocks, the distant mountains, some confused masses of faraway forests, took on a strange appearance under the equal distribution of the luminous fluid.
We resembled that fantastic character from Hoffmann who has lost his shadow.

sentences: Edmond heard the noise of the bed on which the corpse was being shaken; he heard the governor's voice, who ordered that water be thrown in his face, and seeing that, despite this immersion, the prisoner was not coming back, sent for the doctor.
The governor left; and a few words of compassion reached Dantès's ears, mingled with mocking laughter.
"Come on, come on," said one, "the fool has gone to join his treasures, safe travels!"
"He won't have, with all his millions, enough to pay for his shroud," said the other.
"Oh!"
replied a third voice, "the shrouds from the Château d'If are not expensive."
Perhaps, one of the first speakers said, since he is a man of the Church, some expenses will be incurred in his favor.
Edmond was listening, not missing a word, but he didn't understand much of it all.
Soon the voices faded away, and it seemed to him that the attendees were leaving the room.
However, he did not dare to go back in: someone might have left a keyholder to watch over the dead.
After about an hour, the silence was stirred by a faint noise that grew louder.
It was the governor returning, followed by the doctor and several officers.
There was a moment of silence: it was clear that the doctor was approaching the bed and examining the corpse.
The doctor analyzed the illness that the prisoner had succumbed to and declared that he was dead.
Questions and answers were exchanged with a nonchalance that outraged Dantès; it seemed to him that everyone should feel some of the affection he had for the poor abbé.

"I am sorry for what you are telling me," said the governor, responding to the certainty expressed by the doctor that the old man was indeed dead; he was a gentle, harmless prisoner, amusing with his madness and especially easy to watch.

sentences: The old Baron des Ravots had been the king of hunters in his province for forty years.
But for the past five or six years, paralysis in his legs had kept him confined to his chair, and he could only shoot pigeons from the window of his sitting room or from the top of his grand porch.
On sunny days, he would roll his large chair, which resembled a bed, in front of the door.

A servant, behind his back, held the guns, loaded them, and passed them to his master; another servant, hidden in a bush, would release a pigeon from time to time, at irregular intervals, so that the baron would not be alerted and would remain alert.

And from morning till evening, he shot at the fast-flying birds, lamenting when he was caught off guard, and laughing until he cried when the bird fell straight down or performed some unexpected and funny tumble.

He would then turn to the boy who loaded the guns and ask, gasping with joy: In the autumn, during the hunting season, he would invite his friends, just like in the old days, and he loved to hear the distant gunshots.
He counted them, happy when they came in quick succession.
And in the evening, he demanded a faithful account of each person's day.
And they would spend three hours at the table recounting their shooting exploits.
These were strange and improbable adventures, where the boastful nature of hunters reveled.
Some of them had become legendary and were recounted regularly.
The story of a rabbit that young Viscount de Bourril had missed in his hallway made them double over with laughter every year in the same way.
Every five minutes, a new speaker would take the floor:

Noise does not suit everyone, Mr. de Morcerf." At that name, a murmur of astonishment passed like a shiver among the spectators of this scene.

sentences: The servant at our inn was no more than eighteen years old, with bright blue eyes, a pale blue pierced by the two small black dots of her pupils; and her short, tightly packed teeth, which she constantly showed while laughing, seemed made to crush granite.
She didn't know a word of French, only speaking Breton, like most of her fellow countrymen.
However, my friend wasn't doing much better, and although no illness had manifested, the doctor forbade him from leaving yet, ordering complete rest.
So I spent my days near him, and the little maid constantly came in, bringing either my dinner or herbal tea.
I teased her a little, which seemed to amuse her, but we didn't talk, of course, since we couldn't understand each other.
Finally exhausted, she fell; and I picked her up roughly from the ground, off the pavement.
As soon as she was up, she ran to the door, pulled the bolts, and fled.
I barely saw her in the following days.
She didn't let me get close to her.
Then, as my friend had recovered and we were to continue our journey, I saw her enter, the night before my departure, at midnight, barefoot, in her nightgown, into my room where I had just retired.

She threw herself into my arms, embraced me passionately, then, until dawn, kissed me, caressed me, crying, sobbing, finally giving me all the assurances of tenderness and despair that a woman can give when she doesn't know a word of our language.
Eight days later, I had forgotten this adventure, common and frequent when traveling, as inn maids are generally meant to entertain travelers in this way.

sentences: In this vault, the body of poor Renée had already been laid to rest, which her father and mother were coming to join after ten years of separation.

Paris, always curious and always moved by funeral ceremonies, watched in solemn silence as the splendid procession passed, accompanying two of the most famous names of this old aristocracy to their final resting place, known for their traditional spirit, the security of commerce, and their stubborn dedication to principles.
In the same funeral carriage, Beauchamp, Albert, and Château-Renaud were discussing this almost sudden death.

I saw Madame de Saint-Méran just last year in Marseille, Château-Renaud said; I was returning from Algeria; she was a woman destined to live a hundred years, thanks to her perfect health, her ever-present mind, and her always prodigious activity.
How old was she?
--Sixty-six, Albert replied, at least according to what Franz assured me.
But it wasn't her age that killed her; it was the grief she felt over the marquis's death; apparently, since that death, which had shaken her violently, she hasn't completely regained her sanity.
--From a cerebral congestion, it seems, or from a sudden apoplexy.
Isn't that the same thing?
--From apoplexy?
Beauchamp said, it's hard to believe.

Madame de Saint-Méran, whom I also saw once or twice in my life, was small, slender in build, and of a constitution much more nervous than sanguine; apoplexies caused by grief are rare in a body with a constitution like that of Madame de Saint-Méran.
In any case, said Albert, whatever the illness or the doctor that killed her, here is Mr.
de Villefort, or rather Miss Valentine, or rather our friend Franz now in possession of a magnificent inheritance: eighty thousand livres of income, I believe.

sentences: I must therefore dismiss any idea of escape until I can secure a serious chance of success on my side.
If a favorable circumstance arises, I won't let it slip away.
As I walked along the rows of cells, I was able to observe some of the companions of Count d'Artigas, who have accepted this monotonous existence in the depths of Back-Cup.
I repeat, their number can be estimated at around a hundred, based on the number of cells in Bee-Hive.
However, if these inhabitants of Back-Cup are not connected by a bond of race, they are certainly united by their instincts and appetites.
What disturbing faces, what fierce figures, what fundamentally wild types!
They are violent natures, as can be seen, who have never learned to restrain their passions or shy away from any excess.
And,
--this idea comes to me,

Why wouldn't it be following a long series of crimes, thefts, fires, murders, and attacks of all kinds committed together, that they would have thought to take refuge deep in this cave, where they can believe themselves assured of absolute impunity?...
The Count of Artigas would then be nothing more than the leader of a gang of criminals, with his two lieutenants Spade and Serkö, and Back-Cup a den of pirates...
Such is the thought that has firmly lodged itself in my mind.
I would be quite surprised if the future proves that I was wrong.
Moreover, what I notice during this first exploration is meant to confirm my opinion and allow for the most suspicious hypotheses.

In any case, whatever they may be and whatever the circumstances that brought them together in this place, the companions of the Count of Artigas seem to have accepted his all-powerful domination without reservation.
On the other hand, if a strict discipline keeps them under his iron hand, it is likely that certain advantages must compensate for this kind of servitude to which they have consented...
Which ones?...

sentences: People admired the wisdom and vigilance of Idomeneus, who had founded such a beautiful kingdom; and everyone concluded that, with peace established with him, the allies would be quite powerful if he joined their league against the Daunians.
It was proposed to Idomeneus that he join; he could not reject such a fair proposal, and he promised troops.

But since Mentor knew everything necessary to make a state flourish, he understood that Idomeneus's forces could not be as great as they appeared; he took him aside and spoke to him this way: At these words, Idomeneus, already having recovered from his initial eagerness, seemed ashamed of his delicacy.
'You see,' he said to Mentor, 'what the habit of being flattered does.'

'I owe you the safety of my new kingdom; there is no truth that I would not be happy to hear from your lips; but have pity on a king whom flattery has poisoned, and who has not been able, even in his misfortunes, to find men generous enough to tell him the truth.'
'No, I have never found anyone who loved me enough to want to displease me by telling me the whole truth.'
As he said these words, tears came to his eyes, and he embraced Mentor tenderly.
Then this wise old man said to him: 'It is with pain that I find myself compelled to tell you hard things; but can I betray you by hiding the truth from you?'
'Put yourself in my place.'
'If you have been deceived until now, it is because you have willingly allowed it; it is because you have feared overly sincere advisors.'
'Have you sought out the most disinterested people, and those most likely to contradict you?'
'Have you taken care to make the least eager men to please you speak, those most disinterested in their conduct, the most capable of condemning your passions and unjust feelings?'
'When you found flatterers, did you cast them aside?'
'Did you distrust them?'
'No, no, you have not done what those who love the truth do, and who deserve to know it.'
'Let’s see if you now have the courage to allow yourself to be humbled by the truth that condemns you.'

sentences: I believed, however, the traveler replied, that since it absorbed the old Northwest Company, the Hudson's Bay Company found itself without competitors on the American continent.
Madam, Jasper Hobson replied, while there is no longer any significant association engaged in the fur trade outside of ours, there are still perfectly independent private associations.
In general, these are American companies that have retained agents or descendants of French agents in their service.
So these agents were held in high regard?
asked Mrs.
Paulina Barnett.
Certainly, madam, and rightly so.
During the ninety-four years of French supremacy in Canada, these French agents consistently proved superior to ours.
One must know how to give credit, even to one's rivals.
Yes...
especially...
At that time, the French hunters, leaving Montreal, their main settlement, ventured further north than anyone else.
They lived for years among the Indian tribes.
They sometimes married there.
They were called 'coureurs des bois' or 'Canadian voyageurs', and they referred to each other as cousins and brothers.

They were bold men, skilled, very experienced in river navigation, very brave, very carefree, adapting to everything with that particular flexibility of their race, very loyal, very cheerful, and always ready, in any circumstance, to sing as well as to dance!
And you suppose that this group of voyageurs, whose traces we have just recognized, ventured so far only to hunt fur-bearing animals?
No other hypothesis can be accepted, madam, replied Lieutenant Hobson, and certainly, these people are in search of new hunting grounds.
But since there is no way to stop them, let us try to reach our goal as soon as possible, and we will bravely fight against any competition!

sentences: After hearing these words, I exclaimed: O happy day, sweet light, you finally reveal yourself after so many years!
I obey you; I leave after bidding farewell to this place.
Farewell, dear cave.
Farewell, nymphs of these damp meadows.
I will no longer hear the muffled sound of the waves of this sea.
Farewell, shore where I have so often suffered the insults of the air.
Farewell, promontory where Echo repeated my groans so many times.
Farewell, sweet fountains that were so bitter to me.
Farewell, O land of Lemnos; let me depart happily, since I am going where the will of the gods and my friends calls me!
Thus we departed: we arrived at the siege of Troy.
Machaon and Podalyre, through the divine knowledge of their father Asclepius, healed me, or at least put me in the state you see me in.
I no longer suffer; I have regained all my strength: but I am a bit lame.
I brought down Paris like a timid fawn that a hunter pierces with his arrows.
Soon Ilion was reduced to ashes; you know the rest.

I still had some aversion towards the wise Ulysses, due to the memory of my sufferings; and his virtue could not soothe this resentment: but the sight of a son who resembles him, and whom I cannot help but love, softened my heart for the father himself.

A dispute arose between Telemachus and Phalante, leader of the Lacedaemonians, regarding some prisoners taken from the Daunians that each claimed belonged to him. --While the case was being discussed in the assembly of allied kings, Hippias, brother of Phalante, seized the prisoners to take them to Tarentum. --Irritated, Telemachus attacked Hippias with fury and brought him down in a single combat. --Adraste, king of the Daunians, taking advantage of the turmoil in the allied army due to the quarrel between Telemachus and Hippias, attacked them unexpectedly. --He surprised a hundred of their ships with which he transported his own troops into the camp of the allies. --He set fire to it and began the attack on Phalante's quarter. --He killed Hippias, brother of Phalante.

He himself was pierced with wounds. --Telemachus, having donned his divine armor, rushed out of the camp at the first sound of this disorder, gathered the army of allies around him, and directed their movements with such wisdom that he quickly repelled the victorious enemy. --A storm separated the two armies and ended the battle. --Telemachus had the wounded carried away and provided them with all the relief they needed. --He took special care of Phalante and the funeral of Hippias.

She walked quickly for a while; then she slowed down, and her gaze, which she had been directing ahead of her, met the shoulder of the young man, whose coat had a black velvet collar.
His chestnut hair fell over it, flat and well-combed.
She noticed his nails, which were longer than those worn in Yonville.
It was one of the clerk's main occupations to maintain them; and he kept a special little knife for that purpose in his writing desk.
They returned to Yonville, following the edge of the water.
In the warm season, the wider bank revealed the walls of the gardens down to their base, which had a few steps leading down to the river.
It flowed silently, swift and cold to the eye; tall, slender grasses bent together, according to the current that pushed them, and, like abandoned green hair, spread out in its clarity.
Sometimes, at the tips of the reeds or on the leaves of the water lilies, a fine-legged insect walked or landed.

The sun pierced through a ray into the small blue globules of the waves that succeeded each other as they broke; the old, branchless willows mirrored their gray bark in the water; the meadow beyond seemed empty; it was dinner time on the farms, and the young woman and her companion heard only the rhythm of their footsteps on the path's earth, the words they exchanged, and the rustling of Emma's dress that whispered all around her.
The walls of the gardens, topped with pieces of bottles, were as warm as the glass of a greenhouse.

In the bricks, wildflowers had grown; and from the edge of her open parasol, Madame Bovary, as she passed by, let a bit of their wilted flowers crumble into yellow dust; or a branch of honeysuckles and clematis that hung outside trailed for a moment on the silk, catching on the threads.

sentences: He belonged to the great surgical school that emerged from Bichat's apron, to that now-disappeared generation of philosopher-practitioners who, cherishing their art with a fanatical love, practiced it with exaltation and insight!

Everything trembled in his hospital when he got angry, and his students revered him so much that they tried, as soon as they were established, to imitate him as closely as possible; so that one could find them, in the surrounding towns, wearing his long merino dressing gown and his wide black coat, the unbuttoned lapels covering his fleshy hands—very beautiful hands that never wore gloves, as if to be quicker to dive into misery.

Disdainful of crosses, titles, and academies, hospitable, generous, paternal with the poor, and practicing virtue without believing in it, he could almost have passed for a saint if the sharpness of his mind hadn't made him feared like a demon.

His gaze, sharper than his scalpels, pierced right into the soul and dismantled every lie through allegations and modesties.—And he went about like this, full of that benevolent majesty that comes from the awareness of great talent, fortune, and forty years of a laborious and irreproachable existence.
He frowned as soon as he entered, upon seeing Emma's cadaverous face, lying on her back, her mouth open.
Then, while pretending to listen to Canivet, he rubbed his index finger under his nose and repeated, 'It's all right, it's all right.' But he made a slow gesture with his shoulders.
Bovary watched him: they looked at each other; and this man, so accustomed to the sight of suffering, could not hold back a tear that fell onto his jabot.
'She is very ill, isn't she?'
'If only we could apply some mustard plasters!'
'I don't know what!'
'Find something, you who have saved so many!'
Charles wrapped his two arms around her body, and he looked at her in a startled, pleading way, half-fainting against her chest.

my poor boy, be brave!
there's nothing more to be done.--And Doctor Larivière turned away.

sentences: Yes, I know that; I learned it from the servants I saw fleeing the house.
I found out that her name was Valentine; and I have already prayed for her.
Thank you, thank you, sir, said d'Avrigny, and since you have already begun to exercise your holy ministry, please continue it.
Come and sit by the deceased, and an entire family in mourning will be very grateful to you.

I'm going, sir, replied the abbé, and I dare say that never have prayers been more fervent than mine." D'Avrigny took the abbé by the hand, and without encountering Villefort, who was locked in his office, he led him to Valentine's room, which the undertakers were only to take possession of the following night.
Upon entering the room, Noirtier's gaze met that of the abbé, and he surely thought he read something particular in it, for he did not take his eyes off him.
D'Avrigny entrusted the priest not only with the deceased but also with the living, and the priest promised D'Avrigny to offer his prayers for Valentine and his care for Noirtier.

The undertakers had carried out their funeral duties during the night, and sewn the body laid on the bed into the shroud that mournfully drapes the deceased, lending them, as one says about equality in death, a final testament to the luxury they loved in life.
This shroud was nothing more than a piece of magnificent batiste that the young girl had purchased fifteen days earlier.

In the evening, men called for this purpose had transported Noirtier from Valentine's room to his own, and, against all expectations, the old man had shown no reluctance to distance himself from his child's body.
They found him in the large armchair that served as his bed, resting in a gentle and almost smiling sleep.

"Look, said D'Avrigny to Villefort, who was watching his father sleep; look, nature knows how to soothe the deepest pains; certainly, one cannot say that Mr. Noirtier did not love his granddaughter; he is sleeping, nonetheless.
Noirtier did not love his granddaughter; he is sleeping, nonetheless.
Yes, and you are right, Villefort replied with surprise; he is sleeping, and it's quite strange, because the slightest upset keeps him awake for entire nights.
Look, I haven't slept, Villefort said, pointing to his untouched bed; pain does not overwhelm me, I've not gone to bed for two nights; but in return, look at my desk; have I written, my God!
during these two days and two nights!...
have I gone through this file, have I annotated this indictment of the assassin Benedetto!...

my passion, my joy, my rage, it is you who must overcome all my pains!

sentences: She couldn't bear the affront that this wretch caused us, and she asked me for permission to travel.
No, with a relative...
But we are no less losing her, dear Eugénie; for I doubt that with the character I know her to have, she will ever agree to return to France!
What do you want, my dear baron, said Monte-Cristo, family troubles, troubles that would be crushing for a poor devil whose child is his entire fortune, but bearable for a millionaire.

Philosophers may say what they want, practical men will always contradict them on this: money consoles for many things; and you, you must be consoled more quickly than anyone else, if you acknowledge the virtue of this sovereign balm: you, the king of finance, the intersection point of all powers.” Danglars cast a sidelong glance at the count to see if he was joking or speaking seriously.
Yes, he said, the fact is that if fortune consoles, I must be consoled: I am rich.

So rich, my dear baron, that your fortune resembles the Pyramids; even if one wanted to demolish them, one wouldn't dare; if one dared, one couldn't.” “That reminds me, he said, that when you entered, I was in the process of making five small bonds; I had already signed two; would you allow me to make the other three?
There was a moment of silence, during which the banker’s pen could be heard scratching, while Monte-Cristo looked at the gilded moldings on the ceiling.
Bonds from Spain, said Monte-Cristo, bonds from Haiti, bonds from Naples?
No, said Danglars, laughing his self-satisfied laugh, bearer bonds, bonds on the Bank of France.

Here, he added, Mr. Count, you who are the emperor of finance, just as I am the king, have you seen many pieces of paper of this size worth a million each?” Monte-Cristo took in his hand, as if to weigh them, the five pieces of paper that Danglars proudly presented to him, and read: “May it please Mr.
the Regent of the Bank to pay to my order, and on the funds deposited by me, the sum of one million, value in account.

Goodness!
Look at how you go on, Lord Crésus!

sentences: Indeed, half a dozen of these animals had managed to breach the palisade, and, attracted by the smoke, they were approaching the house.
As soon as Jasper Hobson was alerted to the presence of these fearsome carnivores, he ordered the corridor window to be barricaded from the inside.
That was the only exit that was passable, and once that opening was blocked, it seemed impossible for the bears to enter the house.

The window was therefore closed with strong bars that the carpenter Mac Nap secured firmly, after having made, however, a narrow opening that allowed observation of the movements of these troublesome visitors outside.
"And now," said the master carpenter, "these gentlemen won't enter without our permission.
So we have plenty of time to hold a war council.
--Well, Mr. Hobson," said Mrs.
Paulina Barnett, "nothing has been lacking in our wintering!
After the cold, the bears.
--Not 'after,'" replied Lieutenant Hobson, "but, more seriously, 'during' the cold, and a cold that prevents us from venturing outside!
So I don't know how we can get rid of these wicked beasts.
But they will lose patience, I suppose, replied the traveler, and they will leave just as they came!" "You don't know these animals, madam," he replied.
This harsh winter has starved them, and they will not leave the place unless they are forced to!
Yes and no, replied the lieutenant.
I know these bears won't enter the house; but as for us, I don't know how we'll get out if it becomes necessary!” Having said this, Jasper Hobson returned to the window.
Meanwhile, Mrs.
Paulina Barnett, Madge, and the other women, gathered around the sergeant, were listening to this brave soldier, who was addressing the 'bear issue' as an experienced man.

Time and again, Sergeant Long had dealt with these carnivores, which are frequently encountered even in the southern territories, but it was under conditions where they could be successfully attacked.
Here, the besieged were trapped, and the cold prevented them from attempting any sortie.
All day long, they closely monitored the comings and goings of the bears.
From time to time, one of these animals would come and rest its large head near the window, and a dull growl of anger could be heard.
Lieutenant Hobson and Sergeant Long held a council, and they decided that if the bears did not leave the area, they would make some loopholes in the walls of the house to shoot them.

But it was also decided that they would wait a day or two before using this method of attack, as Jasper Hobson was not keen on establishing any communication between the outside temperature and the already low temperature inside the room.
The seal oil, which was being put into the stoves, had solidified into such hard ice blocks that they had to be broken with an axe.

sentences: And Mercédès raised her beautiful eyes to the sky with such infinite gratitude that the count believed he saw two tears trembling there.
"Madam," he said, "I have already apologized to Mr.
the count for having to leave him, and I would ask you to renew my apologies to him.
The session starts at two o'clock, it is three now, and I must speak.
--Go ahead, sir, I will try to make our host forget your absence," said the countess with the same tone of sensitivity.
Mr. Count," she continued, turning to Monte-Cristo, "will you do us the honor of spending the rest of the day with us?
--Thank you, madam, and believe me, you see me more grateful than ever for your offer; but I arrived this morning at your door from my traveling carriage.
How I am settled in Paris, I do not know; where I am, I barely know.
It's a slight concern, I know, but still appreciable.
--We will have that pleasure another time, at least you promise us that?" asked the countess.
Monte-Cristo bowed without answering, but the gesture could be taken as an assent.
"Then I won't keep you, sir," said the countess, "for I do not want my gratitude to become either an indiscretion or an imposition.

My dear count, said Albert, if you don't mind, I will try to return to you in Paris the gracious courtesy you showed in Rome, and I will make my carriage available to you until you have had time to arrange your own transport.

Thank you a thousand times for your kindness, viscount, said Monte-Cristo, but I presume that Mr. Bertuccio has made good use of the four and a half hours I just left him, and that I will find a carriage waiting for me at the door.

Albert was used to these ways of the count: he knew that he was, like Nero, in search of the impossible, and he was no longer surprised by anything; however, he wanted to see for himself how his orders had been carried out, so he accompanied him to the hotel door.

Monte-Cristo was not mistaken: as soon as he appeared in the antechamber of the count of Morcerf, a footman, the same one who had come in Rome to deliver the count's card to the two young men and announce his visit, rushed out of the peristyle, so that upon arriving at the steps, the illustrious traveler indeed found his carriage waiting for him.
